High burden of respiratory allergy in children warrants early identification and treatment with allergen immunotherapy; Respiratory allergy often begins in childhood and most commonly manifests as allergic rhinitis (upper airways) and/or asthma (lower airways). Children with upper respiratory allergy often suffer from coexisting asthma, and other comorbidities ranging from gastrointestinal disorders to emotional/mental health disorders. Consequently, the disease burden is considerable and profoundly impacts a child's daily life. Early identification and appropriate management are important to reduce disease burden, lower the risk of disease progression and additional comorbidities, and protect the child's future well-being. A window of opportunity for halting disease progression may open in the early stages of allergic disease and underlines the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of children at risk. This review offers advice on identifying children with a high disease burden who would benefit from early intervention. Allergen immunotherapy (AIT) modifies the cause of respiratory allergy and prevents disease progression. In clinical practice, AIT could be considered as an early treatment for eligible children, to achieve long-term symptom control and disease modification.
Escherichia coli heat-labile enterotoxin B subunit as an adjuvant of mucosal immune combined with GCRV-II VP6 triggers innate immunity and enhances adaptive immune responses following oral vaccination of grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella); The grass carp reovirus (GCRV) is the most major pathogen that has threatened the grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella) industry of China for years. Though the oral vaccine has many advantages, the current vaccines still do not provide complete protection. Therefor the exploration of new preventive strategies is urgently needed. In this study, heat-labile enterotoxin B subunit of Escherichia coli (LTB) was combined with VP6 from GCRV type II (GCRV-II) via Lactococcus lactis expression system to form a potent oral vaccine and determines if fusion of LTB to the protective vaccine antigen can enhance protection in the fish. The expression of recombinant protein was confirmed by Western-blotting and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. The rare minnow was set as the model for the evaluation of the experiment administrated orally. The immune response including the antibody titer and the immune-related gene expression, and the protective efficacy which included the virus loaded and the relative protection, were thoroughly investigated after the trial. The results indicated that LTB can significantly elicit a higher neutralizing antibody responses and enhanced T-cell priming, activities and proliferation in mononuclear cells from intestine, spleen and kidney tissues when compared to the VP6 vaccine alone. Moreover, the combined adjuvant can significantly up-regulate type I interferon signaling in different immune organs, especially the mucosa associated lymphoidtissue which could not be induced by VP6 along, result in the contribution of the improvement in adaptive immune responses of the fish. In addition, challenge study showed that LTB combined VP6 could greatly improve the relative percent survival of the fish during the virus infection. These results highlight that LTB has the potential value to be a mucosal adjuvant of the fish, approaching for improving the efficacy of vaccination against GCRV-II, which does elicit both non-specific and specific immune responses.

Mucosal IFNλ1 mRNA-based immunomodulation effectively reduces SARS-CoV-2 induced mortality in mice; RNA vaccines elicit protective immunity against SARS-CoV-2, but the use of mRNA as an antiviral immunotherapeutic is unexplored. Here, we investigate the activity of lipidoid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated mRNA encoding human IFNλ1 (ETH47), which is a critical driver of innate immunity at mucosal surfaces protecting from viral infections. IFNλ1 mRNA administration promotes dose-dependent protein translation, induction of interferon-stimulated genes without relevant signs of unspecific immune stimulation, and dose-dependent inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 replication in vitro. Pulmonary administration of IFNλ1 mRNA in mice results in a potent reduction of virus load, virus-induced body weight loss and significantly increased survival. These data support the development of inhaled administration of IFNλ1 mRNA as a potential prophylactic option for individuals exposed to SARS-CoV-2 or at risk suffering from COVID-19. Based on the broad antiviral activity of IFNλ1 regardless of virus or variant, this approach might also be utilized for other respiratory viral infections or pandemic preparedness.
Polysensitisation is associated with more severe symptoms: The reality of patients with allergy; Background: Studying the sensitisation profiles of patients with allergies allows for a deeper understanding of the disease which may facilitate the selection of the best-personalised allergen immunotherapy. This observational, cross-sectional, multicentre study aimed to demonstrate the heterogeneity of the German population with allergies by analysing specific immunoglobulin E (sIgE) patterns towards aeroallergens and exploring the relationship between sensitisation and clinical symptoms. Methods: In total, 500 patients with allergies from different regions of Germany were recruited based on their case histories, clinical allergic symptoms and skin prick test data for aeroallergens. Serum samples were analysed using ImmunoCAP assays to determine sIgE levels for 33 allergenic sources and 43 molecular allergens. Results: Most patients (81%) were polysensitised. Betula verrucosa pollen was the most common cause of sensitisation (59%), followed by Phleum pratense (58%) and Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus (44%). The highest prevalence rates of molecular allergens were observed for Bet v 1 (84%) from birch pollen, Phl p 1 from grass pollen (82%), Der p 2 (69%) from mites and Fel d 1 (69%) from cat. Polysensitisation was significantly associated with the presence of asthma and the severity of rhinitis symptoms. Conclusions: Our findings show a high rate of polysensitisation and emphasise the importance of molecular diagnosis for more precise and comprehensive insights into sensitisation patterns and their association with clinical symptoms. These data may help improve personalised diagnosis and immunotherapy adapted to the needs of individual patients in the region.
Clinical validation of grass pollen exposure chamber in patients with allergic rhinitis triggered by timothy grass; Background: The fluctuation in concentrations of airborne allergens frequently presents a challenge to assessing the efficacy of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) in ‘field’ studies. Allergen exposure chambers (AECs) are specialized medical installations developed to expose individuals to allergens at defined and consistent concentrations under a controlled environment. The aim of the study was to validate the provocation test with timothy grass pollen as well as to assess its safety in the AEC in patients with allergic rhinitis. Methods: In the ALLEC® AEC, varying concentrations of timothy grass pollen were dispersed. Allergic symptoms were measured by total nasal symptom score (TNSS), acoustic rhinometry, peak nasal inspiratory flow (PNIF) and nasal discharge volume. Lung function, assessed through peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) and forced expiratory volume in the first second (FEV1), was used to evaluate safety. Results: The consistency of the test was proved by the stability of environmental conditions, including temperature, humidity and CO2 levels, as well as constant concentrations of grass pollen at predetermined levels ranging from 1000 to 10,000 particles per cubic meter (p/m3). Allergic individuals developed symptoms at concentrations of 3000 p/m3 and above, across all measured endpoints. Lung function was not affected throughout all the challenges. The reproducibility of symptoms was confirmed throughout the tests. The concentration of 8000 p/m3 together with a challenge duration of 120 min was found to be optimal. Conclusion: The study demonstrates that the ALLEC® grass pollen exposure chamber provides a reliable and safe method for inducing repeatable symptoms in patients with allergic rhinitis. This approach can be effectively applied for allergy diagnostics and clinical endpoint determination during AIT.
Consistent efficacy and safety of sublingual immunotherapy tablets across allergens and geographic regions; Background: The clinical development program of the SQ grass, ragweed, tree, and house dust mite (HDM) sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT)-tablets for allergic rhinitis/conjunctivitis (AR/C) included clinical trials conducted in North America, Europe, and Japan. Objective: Data from these trials were analyzed to assess efficacy, immunologic mechanisms, and safety outcomes across allergens and geographic regions. Methods: Thirteen phase III, double-blind, placebo controlled trials in the subjects with AR/C were conducted in North America, Europe (including Russia), and Japan (N = 7763 analyzed). Trials were generally similar with respect to medical practice, target population, eligibility criteria, and efficacy and safety monitoring. Data were analyzed for the approved doses in North America and Europe. Four statistical models were used to enhance comparison of the efficacy end points among the trials. Results: The SLIT-tablets demonstrated consistent efficacy across allergens and regions, regardless of the statistical analysis used. Relative improvement in the primary efficacy end point compared with placebo by using the predefined protocol analysis ranged from 17.9% to 32.8%, 17.5% to 19.3%, 20.6% to 38.3%, and 39.6% with the grass, HDM, ragweed, and tree SLIT-tablets, respectively. The kinetics of specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) and IgG4 responses were similar among the allergens and regions. Local application-site reactions were the most common adverse events for all allergens and in all regions. Most treatment-related adverse events for all allergens and in all regions were mild in severity. The rate of systemic allergic reactions was similar across regions (0%–0.54%). Conclusion: Confirmatory phase III trials for SLIT-tablets in the treatment of AR/C showed consistent efficacy, immunologic, and safety outcomes across allergens and geographic regions.
SQ sublingual immunotherapy tablets for children with allergic rhinitis: A review of phase three trials; Aim: To provide paediatricians with a summary of efficacy and safety of SQ sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets from phase three, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in children and adolescents with allergic rhinitis or rhinoconjunctivitis, with and without asthma. Methods: PubMed searches were conducted and unpublished data were included if necessary. Results: Of the 93 publications, 12 were identified reporting 10 trials. One trial was excluded as paediatric-specific efficacy data were unavailable. The nine eligible trials evaluated grass, house dust mite, ragweed and tree SLIT tablets. Consistent reductions in allergic rhinitis or rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms and medication use were observed with SQ SLIT tablets versus placebo. In a five-year trial, sustained reduction of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms, asthma symptoms and medication use were observed with SQ grass SLIT tablet versus placebo. The number-needed-to-treat to prevent asthma symptoms and medication use in one additional child during follow-up was lowest in younger children. SQ SLIT tablets were generally well tolerated across trials. Conclusion: Evidence supports use of SQ SLIT tablets in children and adolescents with allergic rhinitis or rhinoconjunctivitis, with and without asthma. Long-term data demonstrate disease-modifying effects of SQ grass SLIT tablet and suggest the clinical relevance of initiating allergy immunotherapy earlier in the disease course.

Allergen Immunotherapy: The Evidence Supporting the Efficacy and Safety of Subcutaneous Immunotherapy and Sublingual Forms of Immunotherapy for Allergic Rhinitis/Conjunctivitis and Asthma; Allergen immunotherapy (AIT) is a recognized key therapeutic modality for the treatment of allergic respiratory disease. Definitive studies have provided evidence-based data to demonstrate its effectiveness in allergic rhinitis and asthma due to the inhalation of proteinaceous allergic substances from specific seasonal pollens, dust mites, animal allergens, and certain mold spores. Over the ensuing decades, laboratory investigations have provided objective evidence to demonstrate immunologic changes, including production of protective IgG antibody, suppression of IgE antibody, upregulation of regulatory T cells, and induction of a state of immune tolerance to the offending allergen(s). Tangential to this work were carefully designed clinical studies that defined allergen dose and duration of treatment, established the importance of preparing extracts with standardized allergens (or well-defined extracts) based on major protein moieties, and used allergen provocation models to demonstrate efficacy superior to placebo. In the United States, the use of subcutaneous immunotherapy extracts for AIT was grandfathered in by the Food and Drug Administration based on expert literature review. In contrast, sublingual tablet immunotherapy underwent formal clinical development programs (phase I-III clinical trials) that provided the necessary clinical evidence for safety and efficacy that led to regulatory agency approvals for the treatment of allergic rhinitis in properly characterized patients with allergy. The allergy specialist's treatment options currently include traditional subcutaneous AIT and specific sublingual tablets approved for grass, ragweed, house dust mites, trees belonging to the birch-homologous group, and Japanese cedar. Tangential to this are sublingual drops that are increasingly being used off-label (albeit not approved by the Food and Drug Administration) in the United States. This article will review the evidence-based literature supporting the use of these forms of AIT, as well as focus on several current controversies and gaps in our knowledge base that have relevance for the appropriate selection of patients for treatment with specific AIT.
Key Factors for Success or Failure in AIT Trials; Introduction The first randomized controlled trial (RCT) of subcutaneous grass pollen immunotherapy was conducted in 1954 by William Frankland, who successfully demonstrated the superiority of grass pollen extract over placebo. In 1986, the first doubleblind, placebo-controlled sublingual allergen immunotherapy (AIT) study was conducted on patients with allergic rhinitis caused by house dust mites, which showed a reduction in nasal symptoms to house dust mites after active treatment. While recent large systematic reviews have confirmed the efficacy of both subcutaneous and sublingual allergen immunotherapy for treating rhinitis and asthma, there is significant variation in the results of individual studies. Meta-analyses of AIT studies also reveal considerable heterogeneity. Although the outcome of a randomized clinical trial relies on the effectiveness of the active compound, there are other factors that can influence the results of an AIT trial. The aim of this presentation is to discuss potential factors that may contribute to the success of an AIT study. Possible Factors Influencing the Outcome of an AIT Trial The primary endpoint The success of an AIT trial is determined by meeting the primary endpoint, making it a crucial factor. Although there are instances where trials have demonstrated efficacy on secondary endpoints, while failing to meet the primary endpoint, it emphasizes the importance of selecting the optimal endpoint. For AIT phase III trials involving rhinitis patients, there is a general consensus that a total symptom-medication score should serve as the primary endpoint. Despite its widespread use, the symptom medication score has not yet undergone validation. Additionally, there should be agreement on what constitutes a clinically relevant difference between active treatment and placebo. One approach to estimate the clinical significance of study results is by employing a validated outcome measure that incorporates a minimal clinically important difference (MCID). For instance, the rhinitis and asthma quality of life questionnaires (RQLQ and AQLQ) have frequently been utilized as secondary outcome measures in AIT trials. However, employing the MCID introduces a critical consideration. The MCIDs have been established for longitudinal follow-up of in-patients. Consequently, for the MCID to be appropriately applied, the RCT must include a baseline season. Finally, it is important to note that while meeting the primary endpoint confirms the efficacy of the active treatment, the failure to meet the endpoint does not necessarily negate a treatment effect. Numerous other factors can influence the outcome of the study, potentially jeopardizing its results. The study population To be eligible for inclusion in AIT trials, patients must be sensitized to the allergen being evaluated. Additionally, a relevant medical history that aligns with the sensitization is required. It is evident that room for improvement is necessary for a successful trial. Post-hoc analyses have revealed a clear correlation between the severity of rhinitis observed in study participants and the magnitude of the effect size. Patients with mild symptoms may not experience further benefits from active treatment. Power of the study A well-designed and adequately powered study is essential for reliable results. However, in a survey of 46 subcutaneous (SCIT) and 48 sublingual (SLIT) double-blind, placebocontrolled randomized immunotherapy trials, it was found that 33% of SCIT studies and 27% of SLIT studies did not report a power analysis. Underpowering has been suggested as one of the reasons for a negative sublingual AIT study involving asthmatic children. In particular, when comparing two active treatments, such as SCIT versus SLIT, a power calculation becomes crucial. Quality of the tested agent From a regulator's perspective, the product to be tested should have undergone a comprehensive series of investigations pertaining to its characterization, potency, and stability. These studies should be done using validated procedures. An important factor contributing to ineffective treatment could be insufficient allergen content in the tested agent. When comparing extracts from different manufacturers, a wide variation in allergen content can be observed. In a study investigating the allergen content of grass pollen preparations for sublingual immunotherapy, significant differences were found between the immunotherapeutics with the lowest and highest maintenance doses. These differences amounted to a factor of 31 for protein, 26 - 60 for allergen (depending on the serum pool used), and up to 108 for daily Phl p 5 dosages variations in allergen content can easily account for the heterogeneity in study results often observed in AIT trials. One issue is that the potency of allergen extracts is typically tested using in-house procedures by manufacturers, which renders comparisons impossible. Exposure to the culprit allergen during the assessment phase It is evident that without adequate natural allergen exposure, a study evaluating the efficacy of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) is likely to yield unsuccessful results. Such studies are not often published, but a few examples are available. It is evident that pollen immunotherapy should be monitored during the pollen season. However, the consideration of peak exposure to house dust mites (HDM) when designing a trial is less clear. Although fluctuations in HDM exposure are less pronounced, higher levels of Der p1 have been observed from August to October compared to January to May in some countries. Should a seasonal effect of house dust mite exposure considered? Large placebo effects AIT studies are known to exhibit a significant placebo effect. A survey conducted in 2013 revealed that the average placebo effect in five SCIT trials amounted to 41%. In a field study involving cat peptides, the active treatment group demonstrated a 61% reduction in symptoms, while the placebo group showed a comparable reduction of 59.5%. Similarly, a field study with HDM peptides faced a placebo effect of around 40%, which was comparable to the effects observed with three different active treatment doses. Notably, large placebo effects are common, even in successful AIT studies. Successful phase II versus failing phase III Studies Results from phase II and III studies can differ due to variations in study design, making them not entirely comparable. For instance, a phase II study may have been conducted using an allergen exposure chamber, while a phase III study is conducted in a normal field setting. The patient population may also differ, or a well-designed phase II study may be followed by a poorly designed phase III study. Conclusion There are several factors that contribute to the success or failure of a randomized controlled trial (RCT) assessing the efficacy of AIT. While a successful trial provides confirmation of the efficacy of the AIT product, determining the causes of failure can be considerably more challenging. Essentially, failure does not necessarily negate the efficacy of the tested product. Other factors unrelated to the actual efficacy of the active compound can influence trial outcomes. Study design, inadequate allergen exposure during monitoring, inclusion of inappropriate patients, and selection of inappropriate endpoints can all lead to negative study results that do not accurately represent the true efficacy of the tested agent. Especially when a successful phase II trial is followed by the failure of phase III studies, it is crucial to analyse factors that may negatively impact the outcomes of the latter studies. A significant barrier to understanding the reasons behind unsuccessful phase III trials and negative trials, in general, is the lack of published data. Investigators should be encouraged to publish their negative trials, and journal editors should recognize the value of such reports. In addition, it is crucial to ensure that information regarding negative trials is accessible and documented in trial registers.
FDA Perspective on Environmental Exposure Chamber (EEC) Data in the Clinical Development of Allergenic Products; In 2011, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) within the FDA convened an Allergenic Products Advisory Committee (APAC) to discuss the approach to evaluating efficacy of aeroallergen immunotherapy, primarily in the setting of field (or natural exposure) studies. APAC was asked to deliberate on efficacy endpoints, statistical criteria for clinically meaningful treatment response, and the potential for data from an environmental exposure chamber (EEC study) to inform efficacy. EECs, which are closed units or facilities designed to administer stable and reproducible allergen levels to multiple individuals simultaneously, have been utilized to characterize onset of action of drugs and to assess dose ranging effects. Of interest, aeroallergen levels in EECs often exceed doses found in the real world setting by a wide range (i.e., 5- to 500-fold greater). There are numerous EECs across North America, Europe, and Asia, which have been in development for over 30 years. Most are stationary sites, but a few are mobile and can be set up in, for example, an empty warehouse. Parameters such as size, geometry, and air flow may vary among the EECs. For these reasons, EEC studies are generally conducted in a single center. A typical EEC study collects symptom scores from allergic subjects in increments of 15 to 30 minutes over several hours. Because exposures are identical among subjects, EEC studies of fewer than 100 subjects are often adequately powered to detect a treatment response. In contrast to EEC studies, field studies, in which symptom and medication scores are recorded daily in subjects' natural environments over weeks or months, have multiple centers and may require more than a thousand subjects to be adequately powered to detect an allergen-specific treatment effect. The advantages of EEC studies include their highly controllable nature and ability to assess an allergen-specific response in numerous individuals in the same setting. The limitations are that endpoints are assessed in an artificial setting, isolated from clinically relevant factors, such as presence of other aeroallergens, variability of exposure to aeroallergens due to individuals' lifestyle and behavior, and anti-allergic medication use. The advantage of the field study design is that efficacy of an AIT product is evaluated within real world conditions and addresses the question of does the allergenspecific therapy improve symptoms and medication dependence in often polysensitized individuals. The disadvantages of field studies include its sensitivity to unknown factors, such as variable pollen counts over time and by region and to confounders such as polysensitization, variable thresholds of individuals to take medication, and the burden of daily reporting and retrospective reporting, which can obscure the therapeutical signal and complicate the interpretation of the resulting efficacy data. Although the defined experimental conditions of the EEC allow for direct assessment of the effect of specific AIT, the resulting data may not reflect the efficacy of the product under “real world” conditions that individuals experience during actual product use. Based on these considerations, APAC concluded that EEC data should serve a supportive role. The first FDA approved SLIT product, ORALAIR®, the five-grass pollen extract for sublingual use, was licensed in 2014. Demonstration of effectiveness was based on four Phase 3 field studies and a Phase 2 EEC study. The efficacy results from all 5 studies were similar in magnitude. In accordance with the recommendations from the 2011 APAC, the field data primarily demonstrated effectiveness of ORALAIR and EEC data supported the field study data (see Section 14 of the ORALAIR U.S. package insert). The impact of EEC data in the interpretation of the totality of the efficacy data was greater for ODACTRA®, the house dust mite allergen extract tablet for sublingual use. Demonstration of efficacy was based on two Phase 3 field studies and a Phase 2 EEC study (see Section 14 of the ODACTRA U.S. package insert). Rather than substituting for field studies, EEC studies have evolved to be part of a hybrid design in which the same subjects are first studied in an EEC, and then in an abbreviated field study, which is one approach to advance the role of EEC data. A hybrid study design allows for direct evaluation of efficacy data obtained in an EEC compared to the field in the same population. Recent hybrid studies of birch pollen have observed varying degrees of positive correlation between symptoms elicited in an EEC and those reported during birch pollen season. Study design features that can potentially increase the robustness of EEC data include the use of EEC sessions with placebo at baseline and duplicate EEC sessions at multiple time points. Other approaches to overcome the limitations of the EEC study design include, but are not limited to, hybrid study assessments for other seasonal and perennial aeroallergens, titrating down aeroallergen levels so that they are closer to those encountered in the natural environment, and demonstrating clinical relevance of EEC data (e.g., defining a durable treatment response based on minimal clinically important thresholds for symptom scores). Conceptually and based on this experience, the FDA may consider hybrid ECC-field trials for product development of environmental allergy immunotherapy. .
Benefit and Limitations of Apps and eHealth Wearables in Allergen Immunotherapy; Introduction Web applications (apps), wearables and other personal monitoring devices can improve the management of allergic conditions. They can also enable the registration of their treatment, including allergen immunotherapy (AIT). Although thousands of apps are retrievable from the net, just a handful have been assessed scientifically. Therefore, there is a need for evidence-based and user- centred mHealth apps. mHealth apps can have a variety of features including medication reminders, educational content, games, symptom diaries, electronic sensors and/ or patient self-tracking dashboards. Other emerging features include voice recognition, wearable technology, pollen (and pollutant) sensors and virtual reality. However, few of these features have been tested in AIT. We will review data from studies assessing mHealth apps and will apply these data to the AIT context. Retrospective cohort assessments of prescription databases will not be considered. Some examples of mHealth apps in AIT AllergyMonitor® is an online service that was developed in 2009. It fully complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [1]. AllergyMonitor aims to (i) enable the recording of clinical symptoms, drug use and adherence/persistence to AIT and (ii) monitor the efficacy of sublingual or subcutaneous AIT by patients with allergic rhino-conjunctivitis and/or asthma. Regarding AIT, an AllergyMonitor study assessed 46 physicians, including 18 allergy specialists and 28 general practitioners. The aim was to assess whether the use of an mHealth e-diary improved AIT prescriptions. The authors observed that the use of the app (along with information from componentresolved diagnosis) was associated with increased hypothetical AIT prescriptions, with its potential being recognised by physicians [2]. The AllergyMonitor ® app was also found to improve the precision in diagnosing pollen allergy, using daily symptom monitoring and graphical representations of airborne pollen data [3]. MASK-air® is a mobile health app that assesses the daily control of allergic rhinitis and asthma. Freely available since 2015 on the Apple App and Google Play Stores, it is currently available in 27 countries. MASK-air is classified as a Good Practice of DG Santé for digitallyenabled, patient-centred care in rhinitis and asthma multimorbidity [4]. It is one of the 13 Best Practices of OECD in integrated care for chronic diseases [5]. It is also MDR Class IIa registered and fully complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Several cross-sectional and longitudinal mHealth studies have been carried out in AIT. The first AIT study involved 317,176 days of 17,870 MASK-air users (11% reporting AIT). Days of users treated with AIT displayed a lower median global allergy symptoms visual analogue scale (VAS) than those of users not treated with AIT. This study had relevant limitations since comparisons between days with vs. without AIT were not clustered by patient, not adjusted for potential confounders and did not take different products and application routes of AIT into account [6]. Therefore, a subsequent study assessed only grass pollen allergic patients from 10 European countries (42,756 days from 1,093 patients). The VASs (global allergy symptoms and work) and the CSMS (combined symptom medication scores) were analysed. This study applied (i) clustering of observations by users, countries and seasons and (ii) adjustment for patients' sex, age and comorbidities (presence of asthma and conjunctivitis). Patients treated with sublingual AIT (tablets) displayed a lower global allergy symptoms VAS, work VAS and CSMS when compared to patients treated with subcutaneous AIT or not receiving AIT. Observed results were robust to analyses stratified by country or by pollen season [7]. Consistent findings were observed when assessing the impact of allergic rhinitis in academic productivity [8]. Patients using AIT had an improved school productivity (VAS school, WPAI-AS). Several hypotheses can be postulated to explain this finding, from the effectiveness of AIT to the importance of differences in AIT types. In another study on 269,837 days from 10,860 MASK-air users, AIT was associated with a decrease in allergy symptoms in certain medication schemes (oral antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids). However, this did not apply for other treatments, particularly oral antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids. Nevertheless, we pooled SCIT and SLIT and different data may have been observed if the two forms of administration had been analysed separately [9]. Benefits of digital biomarkers in AIT One of the proposed benefits of apps includes the ability to longitudinally collect symptoms, medication usage and AIT data. This enables the detection of changes during treatment. Data from external sources, including weather, allergen load and air quality reports, can be integrated. Overall, mHealth data are important as [10]: • The allergen exposure is not constant throughout the season and patients often travel. In RCTs, an estimation of the pollen season is available in regions. Geolocalised patients using mHealth report symptoms and medications, and this information can be combined with that from daily individual pollen and pollution exposure. • Observational studies can triangulate RCTs. • The real-life approach allows a large number of patients to be analysed in several studies. • Most patients using AIT need a pharmacologic treatment. In RCTs, there is a standardisation of medication use. Real-life data enable the assessment of all medications actually used by patients. This enables the assessment of their impact on efficacy and costs. • Rare allergens can be studied. • The placebo effect can be reduced by comparing exposed and non-exposed days. • Cost-effectiveness can be available. • The European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (EAACI) is supporting further scientific developments of these measures by installing a Task Force group of key stakeholders in the field. This Task Force has already elaborated a Position Paper under revision by the EAACI ExCom on minimal requirements for clinical and scientific applications. Limitations Several limitations exist for mHealth apps [11], especially when they involve AIT. • It should be noted that crosssectional mHealth studies can only be used to generate new hypotheses. Such hypotheses should then be tested in future experimental and classical observational prospective studies using a “hybrid” approach. • The population tested is closer to the general population than to patients in RCTs. However, mHealth users are not coherent and, as such, do not represent the whole scope of the “real-life” general population. • The quality of the studies using mHealth in allergic diseases is highly heterogeneous and the number of robust trials is still low. Moreover, validation studies of mHealth tools are almost inexistent. Aimed to pave the way for future improvement, EAACI has prioritised this topic and is supporting a Task-Force initiative.
Quantifying the benefits of early sublingual allergen immunotherapy tablet initiation in children; Background: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a chronic inflammatory disease of the upper airway, which progresses into allergic asthma (AA) in up to 45% of children. This analysis aimed to investigate clinical and economic benefits of sublingual allergen immunotherapy (SLIT tablets) initiated early in childhood for the treatment of AR by quantifying the long-term reduction in new cases of AA. Methods: A Markov model was developed to estimate the long-term effects of SLIT tablets on the risk of developing asthma. Key parameters were primarily based on data from the GRAZAX® Asthma Prevention trial and included the age- and treatment-dependent risk of developing AA as well as annual probabilities of progression/remission in AR severity. Healthcare costs were estimated using data from the REACT study. Results: In a modelled cohort of children with moderate-to-severe seasonal AR initiated on SLIT tablets at ages 7 and 12, 24% and 29%, respectively, develop AA during a 20-year period. Additionally, initiation of SLIT tablets at age 5 is associated with a total healthcare cost of EUR 20,429 per patient, whereas initiation at ages 7 and 12 is associated with, respectively, EUR 21,050 and EUR 22,379 per patient 20 years after AR diagnosis. Conclusion: Initiation of SLIT tablets in early childhood is associated with a clinically meaningful and permanent reduction in new cases of AA and lower healthcare costs among children with AR. This finding supports the clinical relevance of initiating SLIT tablets early for children with AR to obtain long-term clinical benefits.

Peripheral blood mononuclear cell transcriptome profile in a clinical trial with subcutaneous, grass pollen allergoid immunotherapy; Introduction: Allergen-specific immunotherapy (AIT) is the only disease-modifying treatment in allergic airway diseases. Underlying immunological mechanisms and candidate biomarkers, which may be translated into predictive/surrogate measures of clinical efficacy, remain an active area of research. The aim of this study was to evaluate Pollinex Quattro (PQ) Grass AIT induced immunomodulatory mechanisms, based on transcriptome profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Methods: 119 subjects with grass pollen induced seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) were randomized in a 2:2:1:1 ratio to receive a cumulative dose of PQ Grass as a conventional or extended pre-seasonal regimen, placebo, or placebo with MicroCrystalline Tyrosine. Gene expression analysis was an exploratory endpoint evaluated in a subgroup of 30 subjects randomly selected from the four treatment arms. Samples were collected at three time points: screening (baseline), before the start of the grass pollen season and at the end of the season. This study was funded by the manufacturer of PQ. Results: Transcriptome analysis demonstrated that the most significant changes in gene expression, for both treatment regimens, were at the end of the grass pollen season, with the main Th1 candidate molecules (IL-12A, IFNγ) upregulated and Th2 signature cytokines downregulated (IL-4, IL-13, IL-9) (p <.05). Conclusion: Peripheral blood mononuclear cells transcriptome profile showed an inhibition of Th2, Th17 pro-inflammatory allergic responses and immune deviation towards Th1 responses. Efficacy and Safety of House Dust Mite Sublingual Immunotherapy Tablet for Allergic Rhinoconjunctivitis in Subjects ≥50 Years; Rationale: Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT)-tablets are FDA-approved up to age 65 years. This post hoc analysis evaluated the efficacy, immunologic response, and safety of house dust mite (HDM) SLIT-tablets in adult subjects aged <50 or ≥50 years. Methods: Efficacy data were pooled from 2 previously described randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in subjects with allergic rhinitis/conjunctivitis (AR/C). Conclusions: Efficacy and immunological changes with HDM SLIT-tablets in subjects ≥50 years are consistent with younger subjects, suggesting an adequate immunological and clinical response in older patients. Grass Allergy and Risk of Anaphylaxis During Subcutaneous Immunotherapy; Rationale: Anaphylaxis is a rare but dangerous potential side-effect during subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). Methods: A retrospective chart review of patients receiving SCIT at large Academic Institute in Portland, OR, was performed between the years 2020-2022. Simple descriptive statistics were utilized to compare the rates of anaphylaxis during or outside of grass allergy season in the Pacific Northwest. We considered grass allergy season from April-July. Results: Out of 118 patients receiving SCIT with grass allergy, 66 (55.9%) were female, 48 male (40.7%), 2 (1.7%) non-binary and 2 (1.7%) declined to disclose. Ten (76.9%) anaphylactic events occurred in women and women were more likely to have anaphylaxis than men (OR 4.1). Anaphylaxis occurred more often during grass allergy season (8/13, 61.5%) and if still on build-up during grass allergy season (6/8, 75%). Conclusions: Anaphylaxis was more common during grass allergy season in those on SCIT, among women, and those titrating up on their dosing. Grass pollen allergen immunotherapy: Safety and efficacy profile; Introduction: Respiratory allergies to grass pollens are very widespread in the general population and the treatment is generally symptomatic which sometimes remains insufficient. First in vitro and in vivo evaluation of recombinant IL-1β protein as a potential immunomodulator against viral infection in fish; IL-1β is an important proinflammatory cytokine with multifaceted modulatory roles in immune responses. In fish, recombinant IL-1β has been employed in the control of bacterial diseases, while the antiviral mechanisms of IL-1β remain largely unknown, and the efficacy of recombinant IL-1β as an immunomodulator to prevent viral diseases is still not determined. This study evaluated the immunomodulatory effects of recombinant grass carp IL-1β against grass carp reovirus (GCRV) in vitro and in vivo. Firstly, the mature form (Ser111-Lys270) of grass carp IL-1β was identified, and its recombinant protein (designated as rgcIL-1β) was prepared through prokaryotic expression. Then, an in vitro evaluation model for rgcIL-1β activity was established in the CIK cells, with the appropriate concentration (600 ng/mL) and effect time (1 h). In vitro, rgcIL-1β could not only induce the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α but also a series of antiviral factors including IFN-1, IFN-2, IFN-γ, and ISG15. Mechanistically, transcriptome analysis and western blotting confirmed that rgcIL-1β activated multiple transcriptional factors, including NF-κB, IRF1, IRF3, and IRF8, and the signal pathways associated with inflammatory cytokines and antiviral factors expression. Expectedly, rgcIL-1β treatment significantly inhibited GCRV replication in vitro. In vivo administration of rgcIL-1β via intraperitoneal pre-injection significantly aroused an antiviral response to restrict GCRV replication and intense tissue inflammation in grass carp, demonstrating the immunomodulatory effects of rgcIL-1β. More importantly, rgcIL-1β administrated with 10 ng/g and 1 ng/g could improve the survival rate of grass carp during GCRV infection. This study represents the first time to comprehensively reveal the immunomodulatory and antiviral mechanisms of IL-1β in fish and may also pave the way for further developing recombinant IL-1β as an immunotherapy for the prevention and control of fish viral diseases.
Prevention Is Better than Cure: Impact of Allergen Immunotherapy on the Progression of Airway Disease; Allergen immunotherapy is highly effective for seasonal pollinosis. Three years of treatment results in long-term efficacy. This disease modification is accompanied by downregulation of allergen-specific Th2 responses and the induction of persistent specific IgG- and IgA-associated IgE-blocking activity. In children with seasonal rhinitis, both subcutaneous and sublingual pollen immunotherapy have been shown to reduce the development of asthma symptoms and asthma medication requirements. House dust mite tablet allergen immunotherapy has been shown to be effective for perennial mite–driven rhinitis in adults and children and may suppress asthma exacerbations, whereas its long-term efficacy has yet to be explored. The success of primary prevention of peanut allergy in childhood by introduction of peanut into the diet during infancy provides a strong rationale to explore whether primary prevention of inhalant allergies and asthma may also be possible. House dust mite allergy is a major risk factor for developing asthma. Preliminary data in at-risk children suggest that sublingual house dust mite immunotherapy initiated during infancy could reduce the onset of multiple allergen sensitizations and prevent the development of asthma at age 6 years. This possibility should now be explored in an adequately powered, prospectively randomized controlled trial.

The KAAACI Guidelines for Sublingual Immunotherapy; Allergen immunotherapy is regarded as the only disease-modifying treatment option for various allergic conditions, including allergic rhinitis and asthma. Among the routes of administration of allergens, sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) has gained clinical interest recently, and the prescription of SLIT is increasing among patients with allergies. After 30 years of SLIT use, numerous pieces of evidence supporting its efficacy, safety, and mechanism allows SLIT to be considered as an alternative option to subcutaneous immunotherapy. Based on the progressive development of SLIT, the current guideline from the Korean Academy of Asthma, Allergy, and Clinical Immunology aims to provide an expert opinion by allergy, pediatrics, and otorhinolaryngology specialists with an extensive literature review. Grass pollen allergoids conjugated with mannan for subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy: a dose-finding study; Background: Polymerized allergoids conjugated with mannan represent a novel approach of allergen immunotherapy targeting dendritic cells. In this study, we aimed to determine the optimal dose of mannan-allergoid conjugates derived from grass pollen (Phleum pratense and Dactylis glomerata) administered via either the subcutaneous or sublingual route. Methods: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with a double-dummy design was conducted, involving 162 participants across 12 centers in Spain. Subjects were randomly allocated to one of nine different treatment groups, each receiving either placebo or active treatment at doses of 500, 1,000, 3,000, or 5,000 mTU/mL over four months. Each participant received five subcutaneous (SC) doses of 0.5 mL each, every 30 days, and a daily sublingual (SL) dose of 0.2 mL. Participants who received active treatment through SC, received placebo through SL. Participants who received active treatment through SL, received placebo SC. One Group, as control, received bot SC and SL placebo. The primary efficacy outcome was the improvement in titrated nasal provocation tests (NPT) at the end of the study compared to baseline. Secondary outcomes included specific antibody (IgG4, IgE) and cellular (IL-10 producing and regulatory T cell) responses. All adverse events and side reactions were recorded and assessed. Results: Post-treatment, the active groups showed improvements in NPT ranging from 33% to 53%, with the highest doses showing the greatest improvements regardless of the administration route. In comparison, the placebo group showed a 12% improvement. No serious systemic or local adverse reactions were recorded, and no adrenaline was required. Sublingual immunotherapy tablets in monosensitized and polysensitized adults with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis; Background: Most patients with allergic rhinitis/conjunctivitis (AR/C) are sensitized to more than one allergen. The overall safety profile was not qualitatively different between the subjects who were monosensitized and the subjects who were polysensitized. Potency testing of allergoids: Development of immunological test systems for quantification of cross-linked, aluminum hydroxide-adsorbed medicinal products; IgE-mediated allergic disorders can be treated with allergen immunotherapy (AIT) inducing immunomodulation via repeated administration of the causative allergen. In order to reduce allergenicity in AIT products, natural allergen extracts can be chemically cross-linked to generate an allergoid, which is adsorbed to aluminum hydroxide to enhance immunogenicity. Currently, only a limited number of assays are suitable for batch release testing of these products at the level of the final product. Accordingly, determination of allergoid content in aluminum-adsorbed formulations represents a considerable option to ensure quality, safety, and efficacy of AIT products. These tests would be a valuable tool for a more comprehensive assessment of batch-tobatch consistency and may allow for comparability of allergoid AIT products from different manufacturers. One prerequisite for development of such an Allergoid Content Assay (ACA) is the identification of suitable primary antibodies. Specificity of rabbit α-grass allergoid sera or a commercially available α-Phl p 5 monoclonal antibody (mAb) that binds to a species-specific epitope present on timothy grass allergen was determined by isoelectric focus (IEF) and Western immunoblotting. High specificity of the tested primary antibodies was identified and confirmed their suitability for the intended immunoassay. Applicable experimental conditions were defined for the ACA resulting in high signal intensities and a dose-dependent signal. The performance of the ACA for quantitative allergoid analysis in the final product was demonstrated, with high specificity as revealed by low or no non-specific signals against other AIT products (from birch, mite or alder) using either rabbit α-grass allergoid sera or α-Phl p 5 mAb, respectively. In addition, the ACA is suitable for demonstrating batch-to-batch consistency and comparability of grass AIT products from different manufacturers. The results of the quantitative allergoid analysis of three different grass AIT products revealed a comparable allergoid content. In contrast, use of the mAb demonstrated productspecific differences in composition with respect to the amount of Phl p 5 in the analyzed products. Taken together, the ACA is suitable to quantify immunologically active modified proteins in complex with aluminumhydroxide, a prerequisite for routine batch release testing and contribute to ensure quality, safety and efficacy of AIT and other immunotherapy products.

Methods: A common effects metaanalysis [1] was applied and justified due to the similarity of study designs, study populations, primary endpoint definitions (i.e., the EAACI recommended combined symptom and medication score (CSMS) [2]) and statistical analysis methods. Wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis: subtypes, diagnosis, and management; Wheat-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (WDEIA) is an IgE-mediated food allergy with allergic symptoms ranging from intermittent urticaria to severe anaphylaxis that occurs when wheat ingestion is combined with augmenting cofactors such as exercise, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or alcohol. In most cases, patients are identified by sensitization to ω5-gliadins in the gluten fraction of wheat. ω5-gliadin-negative subtypes of WDEIA are often difficult to diagnose and may be caused by Tri a 14 (wheat lipid transfer protein), after percutaneous sensitization with hydrolyzed wheat proteins, or, in rare cases, by cross-reactivity to grass pollen. Diagnosis is established based on the patients’ history in combination with serum IgE profile, skin testing, basophil activation tests, and challenge tests with cofactors. Individual dietary counselling remains the central pillar in the management of WDEIA patients. A completely wheat-free diet is a possible option. However, this appears to promote tolerance less than continued regular consumption of gluten-containing cereals in the absence of cofactors. All patients should have an emergency set for self-treatment including an adrenaline autoinjector and receive adequate instruction. More data are needed on sublingual immunotherapy for WDEIA, a potentially promising therapeutic prospect. This article provides an overview of current knowledge on the diagnosis and management of WDEIA including an optimized challenge protocol using wheat gluten and cofactors.
A 5-Year Open-Label Follow-up of a Randomized Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trial of Intralymphatic Immunotherapy for Birch and Grass Allergy Reveals Long-term Beneficial Effects; BACKGROUND: Intralymphatic immunotherapy (ILIT) is a novel, faster alternative to conventional allergen immunotherapy (AIT). METHODS: Fifty-eight patients with allergic rhinitis were treated with either placebo or a combination of ALK Alutard Birch and Grass 1000 SQ-U administered in 3 intralymphatic injections at 1-month intervals. EE414 Health Economic Evaluation of Early Initiation of Grass Sublingual Immunotherapy Tablets in Children; Objectives: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is recognized as a major risk factor for developing allergic asthma (AA). Previous research show childhood AR increases the risk of new-onset asthma two- to seven-fold. Having both AR and AA in childhood increases the risk of asthma persisting into adulthood. This study estimates costs and effectiveness for early initiation of 75,000 SQ-T grass SLIT-tablet, by quantifying the risk-reduction of new-onset of AA in children with moderate/severe AR. Methods: We developed a Markov model to capture the interrelation between AR and AA. Age-specific risk of developing asthma and treatment-specific transition matrices for movements between mild and moderate/severe AR were estimated and extrapolated for grass SLIT-tablet and symptom-relieving medication using the GRAZAX® Asthma Prevention (GAP) placebo-controlled trial in children aged 5–12 years. Together with the treatment effect of grass SLIT-tablet compared to symptom-relieving medication and placebo these constituted the key model parameters. Costs were estimated using previously published data from the IBM MarketScan database. Results: Modelling a cohort of 1,000 children diagnosed with moderate/severe seasonal AR, initiating grass SLIT-tablet at age five compared to age nine prevents 71 incidences of AA, equal to a number needed to treat of 14, as well as 1,220 patient years with AA in the 20 years following AR diagnosis. In the same period costs were reduced by 4,179 USD. Comparing grass SLIT-tablet initiation at age five to six also showed positive results (26 avoided AA incidences, 492 patient years, reduced costs by 1,518 USD). Conclusions: Results suggest initiating 75,000 SQ-T grass SLIT-tablet at age five compared to initiation later in childhood is associated with a clinically meaningful reduction in new AA cases. Moreover, early initiation of 75,000 SQ-T grass SLIT-tablet is a dominant treatment (better efficacy and cost-saving) strategy compared to both later initiation and treatment with symptom-relieving medication alone.

Persistence in allergen immunotherapy: A longitudinal, prescription data-based real-world analysis; Introduction: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a widespread disease with increasing prevalence in developed countries. The only treatment that tackles the underlying causes is allergen immunotherapy (AIT). This treatment is performed through two application routes, the subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT) or the sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). However, persistence during the long course of treatment over 3 years is key for the efficacy of this treatment option. The impaired adherence significantly impacts public health resources. The aim of this study was to assess the persistence of AIT for both application routes. Methods: IQVIATM LRx was used to identify patients starting AIT between 2009 and 2018 with grass pollen (GP), early flowering tree pollen (EFTP) and house dust mite (HDM) allergens. Patients were classified within each allergen category by AIT groups (subcutaneous depigmented polymerised allergen AIT [dSCIT], other subcutaneous AIT [oSCIT] and SLIT) and age (5-11 years, 12-17 years, 18+ years). Furthermore, they were followed up for up to 3 years until the cessation of treatment. Patients, who were still on treatment after 3 years were deemed to be censored. Kaplan-Meier curves of persistence were generated and compared by log-rank tests. Results: The number of patients included in the three allergen categories was 38,717 GP, 23,183 EFTP, and 41,728 HDM AIT. In all allergen categories and for any product group, patient persistence decreased with increasing age class with the difference between 5-11 years and 12-17 years greater than between the latter and 18+ years. The percentage of patients completing the first year of AIT was low, particularly for SLIT where 22.2%–27.1% of patients remained persistent after 12 months. The equivalent figures for dSCIT were 52.0%–64.1% and for oSCIT 38.3%–50.3%. Conclusion: Persistence in AIT in AR was low in this retrospective prescription-based database and was clearly linked to patient age and application route.

EAACI Molecular Allergology User's Guide 2.0; Since the discovery of immunoglobulin E (IgE) as a mediator of allergic diseases in 1967, our knowledge about the immunological mechanisms of IgE-mediated allergies has remarkably increased. In addition to understanding the immune response and clinical symptoms, allergy diagnosis and management depend strongly on the precise identification of the elicitors of the IgE-mediated allergic reaction. In the past four decades, innovations in bioscience and technology have facilitated the identification and production of well-defined, highly pure molecules for component-resolved diagnosis (CRD), allowing a personalized diagnosis and management of the allergic disease for individual patients. The first edition of the “EAACI Molecular Allergology User's Guide” (MAUG) in 2016 rapidly became a key reference for clinicians, scientists, and interested readers with a background in allergology, immunology, biology, and medicine. Nevertheless, the field of molecular allergology is moving fast, and after 6 years, a new EAACI Taskforce was established to provide an updated document. The Molecular Allergology User's Guide 2.0 summarizes state-of-the-art information on allergen molecules, their clinical relevance, and their application in diagnostic algorithms for clinical practice. It is designed for both, clinicians and scientists, guiding health care professionals through the overwhelming list of different allergen molecules available for testing. Further, it provides diagnostic algorithms on the clinical relevance of allergenic molecules and gives an overview of their biology, the basic mechanisms of test formats, and the application of tests to measure allergen exposure.
Anaphylaxis is Uncommon in Clinical Trials of Sublingual Immunotherapy Tablets as Identified by a Standardized Algorithm; Rationale: There is no universal consensus definition for anaphylaxis in sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) trials. Therefore, the reported incidence varies considerably. An algorithm in the Standardized MedDRA Query (SMQ) was used to identify anaphylaxis in SLIT-tablet trials. Methods: Criteria 1 of the algorithm was treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) with narrow MedDRA preferred terms representing anaphylaxis (i.e., “anaphylactic reaction”). Criteria 2 was all TEAEs with broad terms from ≥2 of 3 categories (respiratory, skin, and cardiovascular) occurring on the same day. The criteria were applied to all subjects in 43 clinical trials (all phases) receiving approved SLIT-tablet doses or placebo. Identified cases were adjudicated (blinded to treatment) by medical professionals and were considered anaphylaxis if either criteria were met and included investigator-assessed severe respiratory or cardiovascular compromise. Results: For grass SLIT-tablet, 1 case of treatment-related anaphylaxis was identified in 3984 active-treated subjects and no cases were identified in 2743 placebo-treated subjects. For ragweed SLIT-tablet, 1 case of treatment-related anaphylaxis was identified in 894 active-treated subjects and 1 case was identified in 892 placebo-treated subjects. For HDM and tree SLIT-tablets combined, no cases of treatment-related anaphylaxis were identified in a total of 2646 active-treated and 3024 placebo-treated subjects. The overall incidence rates in active- and placebo-treated subjects were 0.03% (2/7524) and 0.02% (1/6659), respectively. Neither anaphylaxis case associated with active treatment was life-threatening. Conclusions: The applied SMQ algorithm provides reproducible identification of anaphylaxis that can be applied to SLIT trials and possibly to real-world data. Anaphylaxis was uncommon for SLIT-tablets across the evaluated allergens.

Results: Both transcriptome profiling of the standard and extended posology group showed favourable immunomodulatory profiles, with the extended posology showing most pronounced immunomodulation. At pre-GPS and post-GPS strong upregulation of key signature cytokines and transcription factors for T helper type 1 (Th1) and T regulatory cells (Treg) was demonstrated (p<0.05). Key signature molecules for pro-allergic pathways (Th2/Th2A/Th17) were transiently upregulated pre-GPS and showed steady down regulation post-GPS. Conclusions: PQ Grass extended posology showed strongly enhanced immunomodulation towards the Th1/Treg pathway. Pro-allergic immune responses were suppressed and immune tolerance at transcriptome level induced, providing robust mechanistic support for the clinically relevant and statistically significant improvement demonstrated for the primary field outcome of this study.

Compensation of micronutritional deficiencies in immune cells of allergic patients leads to significant improvement in combined symptom and medication score (CSMS) in a double-blind placebo-controlled pilot study; Background: Functional iron deficiency facilitates allergy development and potentially amplifies the symptom burden in allergy sufferers. It was previously shown that micronutrients can selectively be delivered to immune cells with beta-lactoglobulin as carrier (holoBLG), resulting in immune resilience, symptom relief and allergy prevention. Allergen immunotherapy is the only causative treatment for allergic diseases like hay fever and clinical studies focus on the combined symptom and medication score (CSMS, as recommended by the European Academy for Allergy and Clinical Immunology -EAACI) as primary endpoint readout. The EAACI CSMS was assessed in grass-and/ or birch-pollen- allergic women supplemented with a FSMP (food for special medical purpose) lozenge containing beta-lactoglobulin with iron, polyphenols, retinoic acid, and zinc (holoBLG lozenge) in a proof-of- concept study as secondary endpoint. Method: In a proof-of- concept, randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled study, grass-and/ or birch pollen allergic women (n = 51) were supplemented with holoBLG (verum) or placebo lozenges for 6 months in 2019 and 2020. Daily symptoms, medications, pollen concentrations and well-being were recorded by the patients in an eHealth application. These results were evaluated as recommended by the gold standard (CSMS) for allergen immunotherapy studies by the EAACI as secondary endpoint in this study. Results: CSMS during the birch peak and entire season as well as entire grass pollen season improved significantly in allergic subjects supplemented with the holoBLG lozenge by 45, 31 and 40% compared to the placebo arm. The daily symptom score dSS improved by 38.6% for the birch peak season, 35.2% for the entire birch season and 25.6% for the entire grass pollen season (all p < 0.0001). Conclusion: Targeted micronutrition with the holoBLG lozenge seemed effective in significantly reducing the symptom burden in allergic women. The extent in CSMS reduction in this pilot trial is comparable to the effects shown in trials for allergen immunotherapy products. The underlying allergen-independent mechanism provides evidence, that dietary nutritional supplementation of the immune system is one of many cornerstones to combat atopy.
Evaluation of the effect of allergen immunotherapy by clinical and biological markers in patients with allergic rhinitis in real life-first results from Bulgaria; Background: Allergen immunotherapy is a proven therapeutic approach for allergic rhinitis with/without asthma that leads to a significant reduction of symptoms, the need for pharmacotherapy as well as a considerable improvement of quality of life. However, the correlation between clinical and immunological biomarkers in evaluation of the effect of allergen immunotherapy is still not fully established. Our aim was to study the long-term effect of allergen immunotherapy in allergic rhinitis patients based on some clinical and immunological outcomes. Methods: Patients with allergic rhinitis at least two years after a three-year course of subcutaneous or sublingual allergen immunotherapy with either grass pollen or house dust mite were included. We assessed clinical outcomes by using specific questionnaires validated in Bulgarian language-rhinitis control-Rhinitis Control Assessment Test (RCAT), quality of life-Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ) as well as satisfaction with immunotherapy-Satisfaction Scale for Patients Receiving Allergen Immunotherapy (ESPIA). Specific IgG4 levels were measured by ImmunoCAP according to the EAACI position paper recommendations for monitoring clinical efficacy of allergen immunotherapy. Results: We included a total number of 69 patients (male 43, mean age 31.7 SD 12.04, age range 18-56). Allergic rhinitis was well controlled in 53 patients (76.47%). A good quality of life-overall score 0.65 (SD 0.78) and a high level of satisfaction 72.3 (SD 12.9) were found. Immunological examination of specific IgG4 antibodies by Immuno CAP revealed statistically significant higher levels of blocking antibodies in controlled patients than in uncontrolled (p < 0.05). Conclusion: Results confirm the key mechanism of allergen immunotherapy- formation of blocking allergen specific IgG4 antibodies with a long life even after treatment cessation. We highlight the long lasting immunological tolerance due to allergen immunotherapy and the correlation between immunological biomarkers and clinical outcomes.
Trial design for the safety evaluation of a one-strength dose escalation scheme with a birch pollen allergoid for subcutaneous allergen immunotherapy; Background: Subcutaneous allergen immunotherapy (SCIT) with a birch pollen allergoid has proven to be effective and safe. It is approved in Germany since 1992 with a standard dose escalation phase comprising 7 subcutaneous injections using two strengths (A and B) at weekly intervals. Faster dose escalation schemes are more convenient for patients, and such a one-strength dose escalation scheme with 3 injections of strength B is already approved for other SCIT preparations containing grass pollen allergoids. Objective: to investigate safety and tolerability of the birch pollen SCIT allergoid when used according to a one-strength dose escalation scheme comprising 3 injections of strength B compared to the standard dose escalation scheme with 7 injections of strengths A and B and following maintenance phase with 2 injections. Method: The trial will be conducted in Germany and Poland as a multicentric, 1:1 randomized open label phase II trial. Male and female patients aged between 5 and 65 years will be included when suffering from birch pollen-allergic rhinitis/rhinoconjunctivitis for at least 2 years with or without well-controlled asthma acc. to GINA 2020. The diagnosis of birch pollen allergy will be confirmed by a positive skin prick test and serum specific IgE (>0.70 kU/L) against birch pollen. After randomization, the patients will be treated according to one of the two dose escalation schemes followed by two additional maintenance doses. All adverse events will be recorded, and tolerability will be assessed by patients and investigators using the 5-point Likert scale. Results: An accelerated dose-escalation scheme reduces the number of visits to the doctor's office making the treatment more convenient for the patient. This will have a beneficial impact on patients' adherence which is paramount for the (long-lasting) efficacy of AIT. Conclusion: The use of only one strength during the dose-escalation minimizes the risk of mistakes due to the mix-up of vials with different strengths. Thus, a modern and convenient treatment scheme might be provided using the well-established SCIT preparation that is safe and well-tolerated.
Real-life effectiveness of mite, grass and pellitory injected AIT with monomeric carbamylated allergens; Background: Over the years, the efficacy and safety of both injected and sublingual Allergen Immunotherapy (AIT) has been widely documented trough clinical trials. Many reviews and meta-analyses support AIT as an effective and safe treatment for inhalant allergies. In recent years, the need of AIT real-life studies is emerging to counterbalance the difficulty to apply methods and patient selectivity of randomized clinical trials to patients in real-life clinical practice. Method: The present is a real-life retrospective cohort study (performed in Italy and Albania) evaluating the effectiveness, safety and patient satisfaction of inhalant (house dust mites, grass and pellitory) allergic patients suffering from rhinoconjunctivitis and/or asthma, treated for 3 consecutive years with monomeric allergoid injection immunotherapy. Perceived efficacy and satisfaction with AIT, ARIA classification of rhinitis, perceived impact of rhinitis and asthma, number of asthma worsening episodes and drug consumption were assessed using questionnaires relating to before, after one year, at the end of treatment and after one/two years AIT. Results: A total number of 291 patients (169 Albanian and 122 Italian) were enrolled. Patient's perception of AIT effectiveness, as assessed by symptom reduction after discontinuation versus initiation of treatment, was excellent. In fact, overall symptoms score associated to rhinoconjunctivitis and asthma evaluated by VAS significantly decreased over the years independently form specific sensitization (p < 0.01). All patients except seven reported a reduction in rhinitis, as classified by ARIA, from moderate-severe persistent to mild/intermittent. A significant reduction (p < 0.01) was observed in the use of antihistamines in rhinoconjunctivitis patients and in the need of bronchodilators in asthmatics. Interestingly, a significant reduction (p < 0.01) has been observed in the asthma worsening episodes needing the use of systemic steroids. No patient reported severe side effects and only few local oedema and pruritus in the injection site. Finally, in an overall assessment of treatment efficacy, 230 patients reported a complete satisfaction with treatment, 51 were satisfied, 5 very unhappy, 1 unsatisfied and 4 disappointed. Conclusion: In conclusion the study shows that injection AIT with monomeric allergoid was effective and well tolerated to the full satisfaction of the patients.

Sensitization profiles of individual allergic patients in Germany; Background: Several epidemiological studies have shown that polysensitization and the sensitization pattern to molecular allergens could influence in the severity of the allergic symptoms. Therefore, a better knowledge of the allergenic sensitization profile of patients in real life is needed. This information will allow a deeper understanding of the disease which could aid in the selection of the treatment. The aim of this study was to analyze the specific IgE patterns in allergic patients from Germany and to correlate with the clinical symptoms. Method: Five hundred allergic patients from different regions of Germany were included in the study. The diagnosis of allergy was based on case history, clinical allergic signs (allergic rhinitis and/or bronchial asthma) and data of skin prick-tests to aeroallergens. Sera samples were collected and analyzed by ImmunoCAP® to determine the specific IgE levels to 16 main allergenic sources (grass, weed and tree pollen, as well as, animal epithelia, moulds and house dust mites). Finally, and depending on the screening results, sIgE to other related allergenic sources and a total of 43 molecular allergens were also tested. All data collected were processed and statistically analyzed by R software. Results: All the patients were diagnosed with rhinitis and 12% also showed bronchial asthma. Regarding the sensitization profiles, 77% were sensitized to two or more allergenic sources and 23% were monosensitized to one allergenic source. Betula alba pollen was the most common cause of sensitization (59%), followed by Phleum pratense (58%). Interestingly, sensitization against animal epithelia ranked third with a 56% of the total population. The frequency of allergic individuals sensitized to the major birch pollen allergen (Bet v 1) was the highest (82%), followed by Phl p 1 and Phl p 5 (79% and 55%, respectively). However, sensitization to major allergens from Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, Der p 1 and Der p 2, was higher than the main animal epithelia allergens tested. A positive statistically significant association was found between the severity of rhinitis symptoms and the levels of sIgE to 11 allergenic sources and 13 molecular allergens. Conclusion: We obtained a complete sensitization map in different areas from Germany, with global and individualized information on polysensitization to different allergenic sources and molecular allergens. This type of study deepens in the clinical relevance of allergens and their importance for personalized immunotherapy.

Intralymphatic immunotherapy of patients using a modified MicroCrystalline tyrosine absorbed grass product: A dbpc RCT; Background: Allergen immunotherapy (AIT) by the intralymphatic route (ILIT) has been studied for about 15 years in more than a dozen small trials and is currently subject of the large clinical trial ILIT.NU (EudraCT 2020-001060- 28). Common for most of these studies was that native allergen adjuvanted with aluminium hydroxide was administered. The aim of the current clinical trial is to study ILIT using a modified grass product adjuvanted with the biodegradable depot MicroCrystalline Tyrosine (modified allergen MCT absorbed, MATA). Method: Patients with allergic rhinitis due to sensitisation to grass pollen allergens were recruited in Switzerland through online and social media, flyers, and email to University employees. Subsequent to an online screening (www.ILIT.NU), onsite screening included sixty study participants that were randomized to receive ILIT with MATA (n = 30) or with placebo (n = 30). Three ultrasound-guided ILIT injections of 100 mcl into an inguinal lymph node were given on four-week intervals, and the dose administered was 1/15th of the recommended maintenance dose utilized for subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). ILIT-associated adverse events (AEs) were recorded for three days after each injection using an online application. Results: The recruitment method was effective and enabled inclusion and treatment of 60 patients within four weeks of final approval by the ethics and medical agency on January 27th 2022. Online screening started on January 28th 2022, and first patient was treated on February 10th 2022. The ultrasound guidance ILIT procedure was fast, the time with the treating clinician being approx. 10 minutes. The 60 minutes post-treatment observation after first ILIT injection revealed mild AEs in 13 out of 60 participants (22%) and only one (1.7%) moderate AE. The moderate AE and almost all mild AEs were erythema or swelling at the site of injection. No further AEs were reported for the next three days. The injections were never associated with pain. Conclusion: Ultrasound-guided intralymphatic injection of a commercial AIT product proved safe and easy to perform. Further testing of will include clinical efficacy by a combined symptom-medication score (primary), immunological effects by antibody measurement and T-cell assays.

Sublingual allergen immunotherapy: Safety, adherence, efficacy in adolescents during COVID-19 pandemic; Background: Allergic rhinitis, one of the most common chronic allergic diseases, commonly associated with asthma, has a disease modifying therapy, allergen-specific immunotherapy (AIT). AIT can play a significant role in the reduction of clinical and immunological reaction to the culprit allergen, decreasing the onset of new sensitizations, preventing the onset of asthma, and reducing use of pharmacological treatments. This latter aspect is highly relevant for adolescents, a category of patients that frequently prefer to use “as few drugs as possible”. AIT continuation may be difficult in some situations, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Difficulty in accessing hospitals was experienced by many leading to a discontinuation of therapies for chronic conditions, such as allergic rhinitis. Method: We report our experience on the management, safety and adherence to sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) prescribed to 25 adolescents affected by allergic rhinitis (house dust mite (HDM) -8 patients, SLIT grass pollen -12 patients, SLIT parietaria -5 patients), during the COVID-19 pandemic, following EAACI recommendations. The first administration of SLIT was carried out under medical supervision. We used a personalized monitoring approach according to the type of SLIT prescribed and according to the needs presented by each patient, advising them how to recognize and manage a possible reaction. Results: No immediate severe adverse reactions were reported by patients. Between the 2nd and 5th day of SLIT, 4 patients in therapy with HDM SLIT, experienced an exacerbation of rhinitis symptoms, with resolution after the use of oral antihistamine and topical cortisone+antihistamine before taking the daily dose of SLIT (for 30 days). Two patients on grass pollen SLIT and 2 patients on HDM SLIT, with gastric upset after taking SLIT daily while fasting, presented a resolution of the symptom after we advised them to take the daily dose in the morning after breakfast. Five patients interrupted SLIT for COVID-19 infection, until complete resolution. To date, all 25 patients are continuing SLIT, with good tolerability, with an improvement of rhinitis symptoms. Conclusion: We have reported real-life SLIT adherence and safety in adolescents that started SLIT during the COVID-19 pandemic to confirm how SLIT is a winning strategy and the only modifying treatment for allergic conditions.
