Future forms of immunotherapy; Allergic respiratory diseases affect approximately 15% of the US population. Allergen immunotherapy has been a treatment option for diseases such as allergic rhinitis, allergic asthma, and venom allergy for the last 100 years. During the first 75 years, conventional subcutaneous immunotherapy did not change much. However, the last 25 years has seen substantial growth in the development of alternatives to conventional subcutaneous immunotherapy. The addition of omalizumab, an anti-IgE mAb, to immunotherapy offers the potential for increased safety and efficacy. Activation of the innate immune system through Toll-like receptor agonists with and without specific allergens appears to improve the immunologic responses and clinical outcomes in patients with allergic diseases. The use of chemically altered allergens, allergoids, recombinant allergens, and relevant T-cell epitope peptides are all approaches that have yielded positive results. Finally, alternative modes of delivery hold promise, with sublingual immunotherapy rapidly approaching mainstream use in many countries. One thing is clear: the next century of immunotherapy will be vastly different from today's current standard of care. © 2010 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.
The consolidated standards of reporting trials (CONSORT) statement applied to allergen-specific immunotherapy with inhalant allergens: A global allergy and asthma European network (GA2LEN) article; Background: Randomized trials provide evidence to inform treatment decisions. The Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) Statement is a set of recommendations for the reporting of trials. Objective: We sought to assess the quality of reporting allergen-specific immunotherapy trials according to CONSORT criteria. Methods: The reporting of the procedure, randomization, dropouts, strict conduct of intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, and sample size calculation according to CONSORT were assessed in the 46 subcutaneous and 48 sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) blind, placebo-controlled randomized trials published between 1996 and 2009 in English. Results: One subcutaneous immunotherapy (2.2%) and 3 SLIT (6.6%) trials met CONSORT Statement criteria. These were used for the registration of sublingual tablets to the European Medicines Agency. In subcutaneous immunotherapy, 16 (35%) studies reported a CONSORT flow chart, and 12 (26%) provided a description of dropouts. Adequate randomization was reported in 9 (35%) studies, and incomplete randomization was reported in 15 (33%). Power analysis was reported in 15 (33%) studies. In SLIT, 20 (42%) studies reported a CONSORT flow chart, and 16 (32%) a description of dropouts. ITT analysis was carried out in 1 (2.2%) SLIT study, and a modified ITT analysis was used in 1 (2.2%) subcutaneous immunotherapy study and 2 (4.4%) SLIT studies. Adequate randomization was reported in 6 (12%) studies, and incomplete randomization was reported in 16 (32%). Power analysis was reported in 15 (27%) studies. Conclusion: As in other areas of medicine, the quality of reporting of most immunotherapy trials is low, and only 4.2% of SLIT randomized controlled trials met all of the criteria of the CONSORT Statement. Use of the CONSORT criteria should be encouraged. © 2010 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.

Safety and efficacy of two days of rush immunotherapy among patients with allergic rhinitis and Asthma; This study was done to assess the safety and efficacy of rush immunotherapy (RIT), and was conducted in the Allergy Centre of Kempegowda Institute of Medical Sciences Hospital & Research Centre, Bangalore, India. Interactions between upper and lower airway; It is not routine to treat nasal symptoms in asthma yet it should be considered. The airway is a continuous structure extending from the nasal vestibule to the alveoli, with the same pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium along much of its length. Airways disease often does not conform to specific anatomical regions: upper and lower airway disease often coexists, with upper airway involvement often preceding that of the lower airway and even determining severity of disease and quality of life. The nose filters, warms and humidifies over 10 000 L of air daily and bears the brunt of environmental contact as the site of allergen, microbial and particle deposition. Effective mucociliary clearance is needed for good respiratory health: evidenced by defects as in primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) and cystic fibrosis where sinus disease is almost universal. Rhinitis, whether allergic or non- allergic, predisposes to asthma with an odds ratio of 3. Early diagnosis with either removal from allergen exposure or immunotherapy could probably prevent asthma, as has been shown for grass pollen allergic children. Most asthmatics have rhinitis: upper airways inflammation is demonstrable even in those without nasal symptoms. The reverse is also true- possibly since nasal allergen challenge causes eosinophil ingress to both nose and bronchi and vice versa. Seasonal allergic rhinitis is associated with increased lower airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR), treatable by reducing nasal inflammation. The same dose of corticosteroid is more effective in reducing AHR when applied nasally than when inhaled. Most paediatric asthma exacerbations begin in the upper airway with a viral cold. Synergy exists between viral and allergic inflammation: with a high risk of hospitalization for asthma in the allergic child exposed to both relevant allergen plus rhinovirus. The reduction of nasal inflammation in allergic children by regular intranasal corticosteroid should ameliorate the effects of intermittent colds .Large scale retrospective series showed benefits to asthma by treatment of associated rhinitis: including reduced emergency visits, hospitalization or both. Large well-designed prospective studies of rhinitis treatment in asthma are needed as well as studies looking at effective control of rhinitis in asthma prevention.

Effect on cell surface markers following allergen-induced desensitization of human whole-blood basophils; Background: Allergen-specific immunotherapy (SIT) leads to reduced symptoms upon allergen exposure through as yet unresolved mechanisms. Desensitization of basophils to specific allergens during the updosing phase of injection immunotherapy may contribute to the clinical effect of SIT. Here we report a protocol for efficient in vitro allergen-mediated desensitization of basophils in whole blood and the effect of desensitization on the expression of basophil activation markers (CD203c and CD63) as well as histamine release in response to allergen challenge. Methods: Whole blood from grass pollen-allergic subjects was incubated with Phleum pratense extract by stepwise increase of the allergen concentration in the culture from well below to well above the allergen threshold concentration for activation of basophils. Desensitization was determined by measuring the expression of the basophil activation markers CD63 and CD203c by FACS following challenge with high allergen concentrations. Results: The basophil desensitization protocol reported here affected both the expression of the cell-surface markers and the levels of histamine release. Following the stepwise desensitization procedure the whole-blood basophils were not activated when challenged with more than 10-fold increased allergen concentration. Conclusion: We have established a protocol for basophil desensitization. By mimicking the updosing phase of immunotherapy we raised the allergen threshold for basophil activation and obtained efficient desensitization for all donors. We showed that conditions leading to desensitization affect histamine release and expression of different basophil markers alike. Copyright © 2010 S. Karger AG, Basel.
Efficacy and safety of grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) in a North American pediatric population; Background: A number of immunological changes have been previously reported in subjects undergoing specific immunotherapy, particularly changes in allergen specific antibody responses. A phase 3, randomized trial was conducted to investigate the efficacy and tolerability of a new grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT) and its effects on IgG4 levels and IgE blocking factor in North American children. Methods: IRB approval was obtained at all sites and written informed consent obtained from subjects/legal guardians. 345 children (5-17 yrs) with grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were randomized 1:1 to once-daily 2800 BAU grass AIT (oral lyophilisate, Phleum pratense) or placebo (PBO) beginning approximately 16 weeks before and continuing through the 2009 grass pollen season (GPS). The primary efficacy endpoint was the total combined daily symptom and medication score (TCS). Secondary endpoints were daily symptom score (DSS), daily medication score (DMS), and the Pediatric or Adolescent Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaires (RQLQ). Specific IgG4 levels and IgE-blocking factor were measured before, during, and at the end of GPS. Safety was assessed by adverse events (AEs). Results: The mean GPS lasted 43 days (mean grass pollen count 28 grains/m3). 89% of subjects were multisensitized. AIT treatment yielded significant improvements relative to PBO in TCS (26%, P=0.001), DSS (25%, P=0.004), DMS (66%, P=0.006), and RQLQ (18%, P=0.028). The majority of treatment-related AEs were local, application site reactions. Conclusions: We report the first successful phase III pediatric grass AIT trial in North America. Once-daily administration of grass AIT is effective and well-tolerated, representing a new therapeutic modality for children with grass pollen-induced allergy. The effect of treatment on the immune system was confirmed by the changes in immunologic parameters, specifically increases in specific IgG4 and IgE blocking factor.

Efficacy and safety of timothy grass allergy immunotherapy tablet in North American adults; Background: Until now, the efficacy of grass sublingual immunotherapy has not been demonstrated in North America. Carbamylated monoid allergoids as a new therapeutic option for sublingual immunotherapy of mite- and grass-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis - A systematic review of published trials using Lais® tablets; Lais® allergoid tablets contain allergens, which are modified by carbamylation. Due to their modified chemical structure they are suitable for sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). Based on their small molecule size of 12-40 kDa, they can be absorbed easily via the oral mucosa. In this review, the efficacy of SLIT with carbamylated monoid allergoid tablets on the treatment of grass pollen- and mite-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis was studied on the basis of symptom score and medication score improvement. Following a selective internet and databank search, six trials - in part also placebo-controlled - on the treatment of grass pollen- (n = 266) and mite-induced (n = 241) allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were suitable for conclusions regarding the clinical efficacy of allergoid tablets. The primary endpoints in these trials were the decrease in the need for antiall ergic medication and/or the reduction in the occurrence of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms. Following data concerning symptoms and medication recorded in patient diaries, conclusions could be made about the effectiveness and tolerance of Lais® tablets. The average improvement of the symptom score for three trials on the treatment of grass pollen all ergy was 34% in comparison to improvement under placebo. For the treatment of mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis, an average symptom score improvement of 22% became apparent compared to the placebo or control group. The intake of symptomatic PRN medication under therapy with allergoid tablets declined during the course of therapy. Under treatment of grass pollen allergy, the medication score improved by an average of 49% and by 24% in the treatment of mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis as opposed to placebo or control. Only few side effects have been documented in trials and predominantly local effects have been observed. Severe systemic side effects did not occur. On the basis of the trial results summarized in this review, it can be suggested that SLIT with Lais® sublingual tablets is an effective and well-tolerated form of treatment.
Carbamylated monomelic allergoids as a therapeutic option for sublingual immunotherapy of dust mite- and grass pollen-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis: A systematic review of published trials with a meta-analysis of treatment using Lais® tablets; Lais® allergoid tablets contain allergens that are modified by carbamylation. Due to their modified chemical structure, they are suitable for sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) (13, 16, 17, 24). Based on their small molecule size of 12 to 40 kDa, they can be easily absorbed via the oral mucosa (1). In this review, we studied the efficacy of SLIT with carbamylated monomeric allergoid tablets in the treatment of grass pollen- and dust mite-induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis on the basis of symptom and medication score improvements. The primary endpoints in these trials were decreases in the need for allergy medications and/or reductions in the occurrence of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms. Data was recorded from patient diaries regarding their symptoms and medications used and conclusions were then drawn about the effectiveness of and tolerance to Lais® tablets. The average improvement in symptom score in three trials of grass pollen allergy treatment was 34% in comparison to the placebo group. The treatment of dust mite-induced rhinoconjunctivitis produced an average symptom score improvement of 22% compared to the placebo or control groups. Few side effects were documented in the trials and predominantly local effects were observed. Severe systemic side effects did not occur. On the basis of the trial results summarized in this review, we suggest that SLIT using Lais® sublingual tablets is an effective and well-tolerated form of treatment.

Five-grass pollen 300IR SLIT tablets: Efficacy and safety in children and adolescents; The efficacy and safety of five-grass pollen 300IR sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets (Stallergènes SA, France) have previously been demonstrated in paediatric patients. This report presents additional data concerning efficacy at pollen peak, efficacy and safety according to age, nasal and ocular symptoms, use of rescue medication, satisfaction with treatment and compliance. Children (5-11 yr) and adolescents (12-17 yr) with grass pollen-allergic rhinoconjunctivitis were included in a multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study and received either a 300IR five-grass pollen tablet or placebo daily in a pre- (4 months) and co-seasonal protocol. The severity of six symptoms (sneezing, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion, nasal and ocular pruritis, and tearing) was scored, and rescue medication use was recorded daily during the pollen season. Patient satisfaction was recorded at the season end. A total of 161 children and 117 adolescents were evaluated (n = 267). 300IR SLIT was effective over the whole season (p = 0.0010) and at the pollen peak (p = 0.0009). The adjusted mean difference between 300IR and placebo groups was significant for both nasal (p = 0.0183) and ocular (p < 0.0001) symptoms. Rescue medication use was statistically lower in the SLIT group during the pollen season and at the pollen peak (both p < 0.05). More patients in the SLIT group were satisfied with their treatment compared to placebo (83.2% vs. 68.1%, p = 0.0030), and compliance was high (SLIT 93.9% of patients were compliant, placebo 94.8% of patients were compliant). SLIT was well tolerated by children and adolescents. 300IR five-grass pollen tablets are effective and safe during the pollen season and at the pollen peak in children and adolescents with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis. © 2010 John Wiley & Sons AS.
Patch testing in atopic dermatitis patients; The exposure of atopic dermatitis (AD) patients to aeroallergens or food allergens can exacerbate or maintain the disease. Atopy patch tests (APTs) are able to identify these triggering factors and consist of the epicutaneous application of allergens for 48 hours, with an evaluation of the eczematous lesions induced after 48 and 72 hours, according to the reading criteria of the European Task Force on Atopic Dermatitis (ETFAD). APTs show a higher specificity than skin prick and specific IgE tests, since the pathophysiological mechanism of the reaction induced is very similar to that which occurs in AD lesions. The standardization of APTs to aeroallergens has brought a certain reliability to this method, which is not the case for food APTs, in which the positive predictive value must be improved to avoid any unnecessary dietary restrictions. Thus, optimization of APTs and progress in the knowledge of the pathophysiology of eczemas could help to develop new immunobiological diagnostic methods and specific immunotherapy for AD.
Which allergen extract for grass pollen immunotherapy an in vitro study; Background: Grass pollen is a major cause of allergy throughout the world. The only treatment targeting the causes and not only the symptoms of allergy is specific immunotherapy (IT). A number of controlled trials demonstrated the efficacy of IT in grass pollen allergic subjects, most using extracts of multiple grasses but some using extracts of a single grass. The optimal grass extract for IT has not yet been established. Methods: This study is aimed at investigating the IgE-binding pattern in sera from IT-nave patients from central Italy with allergic rhinitis andor asthma caused by grass pollen. A 5-grass extract was used (containing Dactylis glomerata, Poa pratensis, Lolium perenne, Antoxanthum odoratum and Phleum pratense) and compared to Phleum pratense alone, which is the most frequently used single grass extract, by the RAST-inhibition technique. Results: The 5-grass extract showed, by RAST-inhibition, a significantly higher binding compared to the Phleum pratense extract for Antoxanthum odoratum and Poa pratensis, while the two extracts for immunotherapy showed similar binding affinity for Phleum pratense and the non-Pooideae grass, Cynodon dactylon. Conclusions: The use of a mixed-grass pollen extract seems to be the optimal choice when applying specific IT in grass pollen-allergic subjects from the Mediterranean area. © 2010 Informa UK, Ltd.
Important Florida botanical aeroallergens; Florida is home to approximately 4 million allergy sufferers and almost 15,000 individual species of plants. Only a few of these plants produce pollen with documented allergenicity via in vivo/in vitro testing and provocation challenges. Many plant species with proven allergenicity are present only to a limited degree. Furthermore, allergenic plants in Florida do not follow the same pollinating patterns as the rest of the country, i.e., trees in the spring, grasses in the summer, and weeds in the fall. Media outlets that report pollen counts to the general public may mislead patients without appropriate interpretation. This review highlights clinical studies that document the allergenicity of some pollens and summarizes expert opinion regarding other prevalent and allergenic pollens throughout the state. Copyright © 2010, OceanSide Publications, Inc.
Allergen immunotherapy in Iceland 1977-2006; INTRODUCTION: The prevelance of allery and asthma has increased rapidly over the last 3 decades and is now estimated that 25-30% of population in Western industrialized countries show symptoms of allergy or asthma. The aim of this study was to reveal the success of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) in Landspitali from 1977-2006. MATERIAL AND METHODS: During the study period a total number of 289 individuals underwent immunotherapy in outpatient clinic of allergy and asthma in Landspítali. A total number of 169 individuals were contacted, of whom 128 (76%) accepted to participate in the study. The evaluation was based on medical records, standardized questionnaire and skin-prick tests. RESULTS: Patients were evaluated on the average of 20 years after finishing treatment. 118 (92%) patients were desensitized to grass pollen, to birch pollen (30%), cat dander (30%) and dust mite (28%). At the time of the study 67% reported to be asymptomatic or with greatly improved allergy symptoms. Males had better response to AIT than women (p=0.04). Participants with positive family history of allergy and/or asthma in first degree relatives also reported better response to AIT (p=0.02). Furthermore, AIT to grass pollen and dust mite seemed to be more effective than AIT to cat dander and birch (p=0.04). AIT was also shown to reduce asthma. CONCLUSION: AIT for 3-5 years provides significant beneficial effect of allergy and asthma symptoms in patients who undergo such therapy. Finally, it s findings support the notion that AIT may reduce the risk of new allergic manifestations.
Tolerance induction after specific immunotherapy with pollen allergoids adjuvanted by monophosphoryl lipid A in children; Specific immunotherapy (SIT) is a well-established and clinically effective treatment for allergic diseases. A pollen allergoid formulated with the T helper type 1 (Th1)-inducing adjuvant monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL) facilitates short-term SIT. Little is known about mechanisms of tolerance induction in this setting. In a prospective study, 34 patients allergic to grass pollen (25 male, nine female, median age 10·2 years) received a total of 44 SIT courses (20 in the first, 24 in the second) with MPL-adjuvanted pollen allergoids. Immunogenicity was measured by levels of specific immunoglobulin G (IgG grass) and IgG4grass by antibody blocking properties on basophil activation, and by induction of CD4+, CD25+ and forkhead box P3 (FoxP3+) regulatory T cells (Treg). Specific IgG and IgG4 levels increased only slightly in the first year of SIT. In the second year these changes reached significance (P < 0·0001). In keeping with these findings, we were able to show an increase of T reg cells and a decreased release of leukotrienes after the second year of treatment. In the first year of treatment we found little evidence for immunological changes. A significant antibody induction was seen only after the second course of SIT. Short-course immunotherapy with pollen allergoids formulated with the Th1-inducing adjuvant MPL needs at least two courses to establish tolerance. © 2010 British Society for Immunology.
Local and Systemic IgE in the Evaluation and Treatment of Allergy; Traditional descriptions of type I hypersensitivity and its manifestations center on systemic immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated reactions to inciting antigens. Hence, many current diagnostic and therapeutic measures are based on systemic skin testing for allergy, systemic pharmacotherapy, and immunotherapy. Recent developments in rhinology and pulmonology, particularly in defining the phenomenon of local IgE production in various airway inflammatory conditions, have an impact on both medical and surgical diagnosis and management of these conditions. This review includes a discussion of allergy as a systemic disease, current systemic diagnostic and management strategies for allergy, and local IgE presence and synthesis in the upper and lower airways. © 2010 Elsevier Inc.
Effect of birch pollen specific immunotherapy on birch pollen-related hazelnut allergy; Background: Birch pollen allergy can lead to pollen-related hazelnut allergy, due to cross-reactivity via the major allergens in birch (Bet v 1) and hazelnut (Cor a 1). However, it is unclear whether birch pollen specific immunotherapy (SIT) can be used to treat the associated hazelnut allergy. Objective: To evaluate the effect of birch pollen SIT on clinical and immunological parameters of birch pollen and hazelnut allergy. Methods: In a double-blind study, nineteen patients with birch pollen allergy and concomitant hazelnut allergy were randomly assigned to 1 year subcutaneous birch pollen SIT (Alutard SQ, ALK-Abelló) or placebo-treatment (histamine). Reactions upon accidental hazelnut ingestion during the treatment period were recorded in diaries. Eliciting doses for hazelnut and symptoms (visual analogue scale) were determined by double-blind placebo-controlled food challenge (DBPCFC) before and after 1 year of treatment. Titrated skin prick tests were performed using birch pollen and hazelnut extract, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1, before and at various time points after treatment. Grass pollen, house dust mite and cat extract were used as control allergens. IgE, IgG4 and IgG levels in serum were measured for birch pollen and hazelnut extract, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1. In addition, the effect of SIT on IgE-facilitated allergen binding (IgE-FAB) was measured by flow cytometry. Results: Hazelnut eliciting doses and symptoms measured by VAS during DBPCFC did not change upon treatment in the SIT or the placebo group. Reactions upon accidental hazelnut ingestion were less frequently reported in the SIT group. In the SIT group, skin prick test responses to birch pollen, Bet v 1 and Cor a 1, but not to control allergens, decreased significantly upon treatment. Serum levels of IgG4 and IgG towards birch pollen and Bet v 1, and IgG towards Cor a 1, showed a significant increase. IgE-FAB was inhibited to a significantly larger extent for all allergens in the SIT group than in the placebo group. Conclusion: No objective clinical improvement of hazelnut allergy was observed by DBPCFC, though reported reactions upon accidental ingestions were less frequent. Birch pollen SIT induced significant changes in skin prick test, IgG responses and IgE-FAB towards Bet v 1 and the cross-reactive allergen Cor a 1. This indicates that birch pollen SIT may be useful to treat the associated hazelnut allergy, but a higher dose or prolonged treatment may be necessary.
Patient satisfaction with current treatments for allergic rhinitis and asthma; Background: Rhinitis and asthma are the most common manifestations of allergy in adults and therefore are frequent causes of referring to allergy specialist. Patients referring to the specialist often present severe form of rhinitis and can be managed in different ways according to their characteristics. Aim of this Italian study was to evaluate the satisfaction of allergic patients eligible for specific immunotherapy but never treated with it, towards conventional symptomatic drugs. Methods: An overall number of 311 patients (165 females, 146 males, mean are 33 years) was included in the study. Of them, 42% had only rhinitis, 54% both rhinitis and asthma and 4% only asthma. The severity of the disease was assessed by ARIA criteria for rhinitis and GINA criteria for asthma while the satisfaction with each drug class was evaluated by a scale ranging from 1: very satisfied to 4: completely unsatisfied.s Results: The severity of rhinitis was slight intermittent in 18%, moderate/severe intermittent in 36%, slight persistent in 20%, moderate/severe persistent in 25% of cases. The severity of asthma was slight intermittent in 54%, slight persistent in 30%, moderate persistent in 13%, and severe persistent in 1% of cases. The most frequently causative allergens were grass pollen (38%), dust mites (34%), Parietaria pollen (22%), ragweed pollen (17%), and birch pollen (15%). The most used drugs in pts with rhinitis were oral antihistamines (82%), followed by topical steroids (49%), systemic steroids (15%), topical antihistamines (8%), and antileukotrienes (3%). Globally, 67% and 59% of pts were unsatisfied of the treatment for rhinitis and asthma, respectively. Looking only at patients with moderate-severe rhinitis, the percentage of patients unsatisfied by the pharmacological treatment raise to 77%. Conclusion: Patients with rhinitis referring to allergists are mostly suffering from moderate/severe clinical forms and their satisfaction with currently used drugs is not good and the unsatisfaction, worsens in patients with a more severe pathology.
Application of mass spectrometry to the characterisation and quantification of pharmaceutical-grade allergens; Background: Structural characterization and accurate quantification of major allergens are needed to support the development of high-quality products for specific immunotherapy. Herein, we investigate the pertinence of mass spectrometry (MS) to establish primary structure, monitor structural modifications and obtain quantitative data on major allergens. Methods: Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) and high resolution/high mass accuracy electrospray (ESI) MS were combined to determine the primary sequence variations of relevant mite, grass or birch pollen allergens. Purified allergens were analyzed either as intact proteins or following reduction, alkylation and tryptic digestion. Liquid chromatography (LC)-ESI-MS/MS was applied to the detection of species-specific isoforms and quantification of grass pollen group 1 allergens. To this aim 3 target tryptic peptides were monitored in comparison with synthetic peptides labeled with [13C6,15N]Leu and [13C9,15N]Phe used for calibration. Results: In a first MS study, group 1 pollen allergens from five different Pooideae species were shown to exhibit significant intra-and inter-species primary sequence variability. They also displayed variations in proline hydroxylation, N-glycosylation motifs and O-glycosylation. Two MS-assays were consequently developed to monitor a five grass mix vaccine, namely (i) an identity test detecting species-specific group 1-derived peptides, that demonstrated the presence of components from all species in the mix and (ii) an assay for quantifying all the group 1 isoforms, that confirmed batch consistency. In a second study, variants of the house dust mite allergen Der p 2 were characterized in pharmaceutical-grade material, showing the relative contribution of Der p 2.0101, 2.0105, 2.0109 and 2.0110 isoforms. In a third MS study, a recombinant Bet v 1α product intended for a phase III clinical trial was characterized. Primary structure was entirely confirmed as well as low levels of degradation products. Conclusion: MS represents a very suitable approach for in-depth characterization and quantification of pharmaceutical grade relevant allergens intended for specific immunotherapy.

Safety of sublingual immunotherapy for treatment of patients with severe asthma; Introduction: Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) has been established as an effective treatment for allergic rhinoconjunctivitis in adults, with fewer reported systemic adverse reactions than subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). Definitive evidence for a benefit of SLIT in the treatment asthma is emerging. Currently patients with the most severe asthma (FEV1 < 70% predicted) are excluded from receiving immunotherapy (IMT) in trials and clinical practice guidelines. To date, no data has been published regarding the safety of SLIT in these patients. We describe a series of nine patients with postbronchodilator FEV1 of between 30 and 66% predicted who have received SLIT for several indications. Methods: Nine patients receiving SLIT with an FEV1 < 70% predicted prior to starting IMT were identified from pharmacy, hospital and departmental databases at three sites. There were five female and four male patients identified, with ages ranging from 33 to 65 years. Allergens used included house dust mite (HDM) only (five patients), HDM and grass pollen (three patients), and HDM, grass pollen and cat dander (one patient). Clinician interviews and retrospective review of medical records were undertaken to assess for occurrence of side effects, which were graded according to the recommendations of published guidelines for standardisation of IMT trials. Data regarding treatment interruption and increase in asthma rescue medication use was also collected. Results: No systemic side effects were reported in any of the nine patients. No patients required treatment interruption or modification as a consequence of any adverse reactions to SLIT. Asthma rescue medication use was not increased in any of the patients. Conclusion: In this highly selected group of nine patients with FEV1 < 70% predicted, SLIT has been safely administered without any systemic side effects or exacerbations of asthma as assessed by rescue medication use. Further prospective studies are warranted to investigate the safety of SLIT in the population with FEV1 < 70% predicted.

Recombinant hypoallergenic variants of Phl p 6: Candidates for allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: Phl p 6 is a major allergen of Timothy grass (Phleum pratense). Group 6 allergens have been found only in Timothy and Kentucky blue grass so far. However, despite the observed structural similarity of Phl p 6 and the Phl p 5 N-terminus, immunological differences resulting from unique Phl p 6 epitopes can be observed. Therefore recombinant Phl p 6 has been used in clinical trials of allergen-specific immunotherapy as part of a cocktail of recombinant allergens with native fold. Hypoallergenic variants are believed to further improve allergen-specific immunotherapy. Methods: A set of variants of Phl p 6 with mutations at proline sites were constructed and expressed in E. coli. The purified proteins were compared with physicochemical methods such as SDS-PAGE, UV/vis-spectroscopy, size-exclusion chromatography and multiple angle light-scattering, as well as immunological methods such as IgE-binding assays, basophil activation tests and T-cell stimulation assays. Results: The mutation of proline residues preferably located in loops connecting adjacent α-helices resulted in molecules with decreased IgE-binding. Deletion of proline 29 and 30 proved to have the strongest effect on IgE-reactivity, whereas the mutation of proline 101 had almost no effect. A further reduction of IgE-binding could be obtained by combining multiple proline mutations. Combining deletions of P29 and P30 with mutations of P57 and/or P79 showed a strong hypoallergenic effect. Combination mutants that carry a modification of P57 were found to consist of a mixture of monomers and dimers. In contrast those mutations that maintain P57 and have mutations at P79 are monomeric molecules with excellent physicochemical and hypoallergenic characteristics. Conclusion: A hypoallergenic Phl p 6 variant with mutations of prolines at position 29, 30 and 79 is an excellent candidate for allergen-specific immunotherapy. This variant can be produced with high yield in E. coli and the purified protein meets the high demands made for recombinant therapeutics.

Ultra-short preseasonal immunotherapy of depiquick grass pollen extract compared to placebo in patients with type-I allergic rhinoconjunctivitis; Background: This clinical trial evaluates in a prospective, controlled, multicenter study an ultra-short preseasonal rush immunotherapy with a depigmented and glutaraldehyde polymerized allergenic extract of grass pollen (Depiquick Grass Mix) versus placebo in patients with rhinitis and/or rhinoconjunctivitis with/without allergic asthma caused by clinical relevant sensitisation against grass pollen. Efficacy and safety evaluation of the first and second treatment course will be presented. Methods: In the first treatment year 148 patients with a mean age of 33 years were treated 8 weeks before start of the grass pollen season with seven injections of 1000 DPP/ml of grass pollen extract (1 DPP is the result of depigmenting and polymerising 1 HEPL of allergenic extract.) administered within 5 weeks or with placebo. At day one 0.2 ml followed by 0.3 ml after 30 min were administered as initial up-dosing and followed by 0.5 ml at weeks 1-5 as maintenance treatment. In the second treatment year 146 patients were still within the study for another treatment course. The combined symptom and medication score for rhinitis and/or rhinoconjunctivitis was evaluated using ediaries based on software displaying a questionnaire with single questions on allergic symptoms and rescue medication. Results: After the first treatment course the median time weighted AUC of the combined symptom and medication score was 7.01 for placebo and 5.45 for actively treated patients a significant (P < 0.005) reduction of 22%. This was mainly due to a significant reduction of concomitant rhinitis/rhinoconjunctivitis medication consumption by 44% (P < 0.02). After the second treatment course median time weighted AUC of the combined symptom and medication score was 6.6 for placebo and 4.25 for actively treated patients a significant (P = 0.006) reduction of 36%. The medication consumption was reduced by 65% (P < 0.001) and the symptom score by 18% (P < 0.032). During first pollen season patients of the placebo group experienced 8.1% well day compared to 17.4% of well days in the Depiquick group and during the second season 9.2% and 21.4% respectively. Mild grade 1 systemic reactions occurred in 10.7% patients of the Depiquick group and in 6.7% patients of the placebo group. Conclusion: Ultra-short SIT with Depiquick grass pollen extract is clinically effective and safe already after six full doses. A second treatment course leads to further reduction of the combined symptom and medication score.
Efficacy and safety of grass monomeric allergoid sublingual immunotherapy: A randomised study comparing two different treatment regimens versus drug therapy alone; Background: Monomeric allergoid sublingual immunotherapy (allergoid SLIT) proved to be well tolerated, safe and effective in patients with respiratory allergy. A drawback is that the achievement of a clinical benefit using a standard regimen requires a long time before efficacy may be appreciated. Aim of this study was to investigate whether different regimens of allergoid SLIT (i.e. perennial versus preseasonal) may affect the clinical outcome. Methods: Thirty-three adult patients (mean age 29 ± 10.1 years, 13 F) with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with/without mild intermittent asthma were enrolled into the study and randomised to receive either allergoid SLIT with a perennial regimen (group 1: 10 patients, 1000 AU/week for 2 years, for a total amount of 100 000 UA) or allergoid SLIT with a pre-seasonal regimen (group 2: 11 patients, 5000 AU/week for 10 weeks/year for 2 years, for a total amount of 104 000 UA) or drug therapy alone (group 3: 11 patients). At baseline and at the end of the second pollen season a Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) was performed to assess the patients' well-being. Symptom score (sneezing, rhinorrea, nasal congestion, ocular symptoms, cough, asthma symptoms) and drug consumption (antihistamines, broncodilators, nasal, bronchial and oral corticosteroids) were also evaluated with monthly diary cards. Adverse reactions (ARs) were recorded. Results: One patient of group 1 dropped-out after the randomisation because of two mild ARs (paresthesia at the lips and sorethroat with burning). The statistical analysis was thus performed on 32 patients. There was a significant VAS improvement in both group 1 and 2 after one and 2 years of treatment compared to the baseline and group 3 values (P < 0.05). Furthermore, group 1 and 2 patients had less symptoms in comparison to group 3 at the second year, being the difference statistically significant (P < 0.05). In addition there was a significant reduction of drug consumption in group 1 and 2 versus group 3 at the second year (P < 0.05). No severe AR has been observed. Conclusion: Both perennial and pre-seasonal grass allergoid SLIT showed to be effective, safe and well tolerated.
Comparison of efficacy of conventional subcutaneous immunotherapy and ultra-short subcutaneous immunotherapy containing monophosphoryl lipid a (MPL): Results of a multicentre observational study after 2 years of treatment; Background: Greater understanding of the disease process in allergic conditions has allowed the development of specific immunotherapies which target the underlying pathology. This multicentre post marketing trial compared the efficacy and tolerability of two regimens: conventional SCIT and ultra-short SCIT containing the adjuvant MPL with only 4 pre-seasonal injections per year. Data after 1 year of treatment were presented previously. Methods: Total of 215 patients (78 with grass and 137 with tree pollen-related rhinoconjunctivitis and/or asthma) were enrolled. Inclusion criteria were a rhino-conjunctivitis severity score of ≥5 and an asthma severity score of 1 or 2. Patients received conventional SCIT (as a varying regimen of multiple injections) or ultra-short SCIT containing MPL (as four pre-seasonal injections). Primary outcomes were a global rating score recorded by the physician and a patient score derived from a diary completed during the pollen season. The symptom scores ranged from 0 to 3 (no symptoms to severe symptoms) and were recorded for rhinitis, conjunctivitis, and pulmonary symptoms during the pollen seasons. Data were analysed for non-inferiority using the maximum likelihood method for longitudinal data. Adverse events were recorded by the physician. Results: After the second treatment year, data was available for 145 patients. Regular use of symptomatic medication was reduced in both groups during the tree pollen and grass pollen season. Non-inferiority of ultra-short SCIT containing MPL compared with conventional SCIT was demonstrated in the scores for grass pollen-related rhinitis, conjunctivitis, and pulmonary symptoms and for tree pollen-related rhinitis and conjunctivitis after the second treatment year. The incidence of local adverse events was comparable for the conventional SCIT and ultra-short SCIT containing MPL groups. Conclusion: This ongoing multicentre trial demonstrated symptom reduction for conventional SCIT and ultra-short SCIT containing the adjuvant MPL (four pre-seasonal injections) during the second pollen season after the second treatment. The reduction in use of symptomatic medication was comparable for both groups. Both treatment regimens were well tolerated and showed comparable safety profiles.

Lack of association between clinical efficacy and cellular immune responses in the blood during grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: The efficacy of a 300-IR 5-grass-pollen SLIT tablet on rhinoconjonctivitis symptoms was confirmed in a double blind, placebo controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber (ACC). We took advantage of this study to inquire whether changes in basophil activation and T cell responses can be used as biomarkers predicting efficacy. Methods: Changes in immunological markers were investigated in 82 patients with grass pollen-related allergic rhinoconjunctivitis who received active or placebo tablets sublingually once a day for four months. An allergen challenge with grass pollen was performed in the Vienna Challenge Chamber (VCC) at baseline, after 1 week, and after 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment. Blood samples were collected before treatment and after 2 and 4 treatment months for assessment of basophil activation (based on CD203c expression) and T cell responses (looking at proliferation, pheno-type, cytokine production and gene expression). Results: SLIT with a 5-grass-pollen tablet led to significant improvement (versus placebo) of 29.8% for the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) at end point. Clinical responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. No changes in basophil activation and T-cell proliferation were noticed for active and placebo groups in response to either the extract, Dac g 1 or Dac g 5 allergens, during treatment. Higher expression of Treg markers (eg Foxp 3) and lower expression of molecules associated with a Th1/Th2 profile were observed during treatment for both active and placebo groups. PMBCs from patients exposed to active treatment (versus placebo) displayed a lower production of TNF-alpha and a higher expression of IFN-gamma, with no differences between responders and non responders. All patients with a high symptom score before treatment responded to SLIT. However, neither basophil activation nor levels of T cell proliferation prior to treatment were predictive of efficacy. Conclusion: Basophil activation and T cell responses measured in the blood are not predictive of clinical responses induced by SLIT. Our results do not preclude that changes in cellular responses monitored in target respiratory mucosae can account for SLIT efficacy.
Heterogeneity of antibody responses among clinical responders following grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy; Background: Biomarkers of clinical efficacy are of major interest to monitor patients under specific sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT). To identify such surrogates, we investigated seric and mucosal antibody responses in the context of a randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled study conducted in an allergen challenge chamber. Methods: Changes in titres and affinity of allergen-specific IgE, IgG1-4, IgM and IgA were monitored in serum and nasal secretions in a cohort of 82 grass pollen allergic patients receiving once daily a sublingual 300IR grass pollen tablet or a placebo for 4 months. Average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) was evaluated before and after 1 week, 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment, during allergen challenges in a pollen chamber. Results: A significant clinical response was observed in the group receiving the active treatment. The latter was documented in patients exhibiting distinct patterns of IgE sensitization (i.e. narrow, intermediate, broad) against Phl p 1 to 12 allergens. No neosensitization to grass pollen allergens was observed in the course of SLIT. Responders were defined as the 25% of patients with the highest relative improvement in symptom score from baseline, corresponding to at least a 48.9% decrease of ARTSS after treatment. Comparing antibody responses from patients belonging to each of the four following groups: Placebo responders/Placebo non responders/Active responders/Active non responders, we could establish that (i) Placebo responders exhibit clear grass pollen-specific antibody responses in nasal mucosa and (ii) Active responders are heterogeneous, encompassing both 'immunoreactive' patients with strong grass pollen-specific IgG, IgE and IgG4 responses (possibly blocking antibodies) induced during SLIT, as well as 'non immunoreactive' responders with no detectable immune responses distinguishing them from patients receiving placebo. Importantly, patients with high symptoms scores at inclusion were all improved under SLIT, although specific IgE levels prior to treatment were not predictive. Conclusion: SLIT with a grass pollen extract is similarly efficacious in patients exhibiting sensitization to single or multiple grass pollen allergens. Responders include both patients with strong seric allergen-specific antibody responses or lacking such responses. The latter observation suggests that additional immune mechanisms distinct from blocking antibodies are involved in SLIT efficacy.
Determination of sulfidoleukotrienes production in patients with atopic dermatitis; Atopic dermatitis (AD) is still the most common skin disorder in children and affects 80-90% of the children younger than 5 years. Also, children with AD have the highest incidence of food allergy. It is now apparent that food hypersensitivity plays a significant pathogenic role in up to 40% of children with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis. A number of investigations have shown the guiding role of inflammation, and particularly of leukotrienes (LT) in allergy development. Sulfido-leukotrienes (sLT) are important mediators in allergic diseases that are synthesized after allergen-specific stimulation. These newly-formed mediators show powerful pro-inflammatory activities inducing oedema, increased vascular permeability, mucous secretion, smooth muscle contraction and chemotaxis of target cells. Cellular antigen stimulation test (CAST) was adapted for the quantitative determination of sulfidoleukotrienes release after in vitro stimulation of leukocytes with specific antigens. In this study, we assessed the diagnostic sensitivity of CAST technique after food and inhalant allergen stimulation in patients with atopic dermatitis. Fifty-three children at the age from 9 months to 14 years with a history of hypersensitivity reactions to inhalant and food allergens were studied. We tested the most frequent allergens connected with AD such as: Der p, Der f, grass pollen, ragweed pollen, birch pollen, cow milk, eggs, soya and wheat. Of all cases, 63% (25/40) of patients had CAST test positive to Der p, 65% (15/23) of patients to Der f, 22% (2/ 9) of patients to grass pollen, 25% (2/8) of patients to ragweed pollen and 29% (2/7) of patients to birch pollen. Our results also show that CAST test was positive in 29% (10/34) of patients with allergy to cow milk, 60% (24/40) of patients to eggs, 50% (5/10) of patients to soya and 38% (6/16) of patients to wheat. Findings in this study suggest that CAST test used for confirmation of allergy status in children with AD is more sensitive to allergens such as Der p, Der f, eggs and soya, than to other tested allergens.

Grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy tablets improve QoL in a paediatric population; Background: Cochrane Reviews have been carried out prior to 2004 on the efficacy of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) in both adult and paediatric populations (Wilson et al, 2003). These studies showed significant improvements in symptoms of allergic rhinitis and reductions in medication required. A study (Durham, 2008) concluded that on the basis of currently available data SLIT and SCIT were of equal efficacy. In January 2009 treatment with Timothy grass SLIT tablets 75 000 SQ-T was commenced in a group of 20 paediatric patients, aged 6-16 years of age and QoL was monitored throughout the first year of treatment. Methods: Patients selected for SLIT were under 16 years of age at commencement of treatment and had severe SAR, which was resistant to conventional medication + documented grass pollen sensitisation, confirmed by positive Skin Prick Testing +/-positive specific IgE results to grass pollens. No patients had undergone immunotherapy previously. Efficacy assessments, utilising visual analogue scales and QoL, were carried out weekly for all patients throughout the first 8 months. Rescue medication usage was recorded throughout the season. An end of season rating was given by each family. Results: Every patient, who completed the season, included in this audit, achieved markedly reduced severity of rhinitis symptoms and there were reported high levels of patient satisfaction with some dramatic improvements reported in the children's QoL. There were also improved conjunctivitis scores in some patients with moderate - severe vernal conjunctivitis. There were a reduced number of seasonal asthma exacerbations. Conclusion: Using Timothy Grass SLIT treatment for those paediatric patients with SAR symptoms resistant to conventional medication regimes has proven beneficial as shown in the improved QoL and the reduction in standard medication required. There were benefits in having a group of 20 children all starting treatment at the same time and from the same area of the country. The pollen counts were obtained to compare symptom scoring with them and demonstrated that those patients with previously unmanaged SAR had much better control. Patients also utilised their questionnaires to comment on other family members' symptoms being present when theirs were not, contrary to their normal seasonal history. Eighteen of the 20 children who started treatment in 2009 will be continuing into a second year of treatment with SLIT.

Biologic potency by skin prick testing (SPT) of US diagnostic allergen extracts of cat and Bermuda grass pollen are two-fold higher compared to European and Mexican extracts; Background: In a previous study ELISA inhibition (CBER/FDA competition ELISA) testing of Bermuda grass (BG) and cat diagnostic extracts of three European manufacturers showed relative potencies between 5% and 25% (BG) and 2.1- 29 Fel d 1 Units/ml (cat) in comparison to the FDA standard of 10.000 BAU/ml and 18 Fel d 1 Units/ml. Here we report a comparative study of the biologic potency using quantitative SPT. Methods: Diagnostic extracts of BG and cat from six different manufacturers (two Mexican, three European, 1 US = 10.000 BAU/ml reference) were tested in 21 and 14 patients with SPT as a concentrate and in two serial two-fold dilutions. All extracts and dilutions were applied in quadruplicate during two SPT sessions on the forearms of subjects with allergic rhinitis, who had tested positive to BG or cat in a routine SPT. Results: Most extracts showed a good dose-response in wheal size for the concentrate in comparison with the two dilutions (steep part of the curve). The Wilcoxon test for linked random samples was used in each group to investigate whether the distribution of the Reference Extract differed from each of the test extracts to a statistically significant degree (test level α = 0.05). BG: European (two-sided asymptotic significance P = 0.001-0.005) and Mexican (P = 0.005-0.022) extracts were less potent than the reference extract. Cat: only Eur2 (P = 0.013) and Mex2 (P = 0.005) were less potent. Expressing the potency relative to the 10.000 BAU/ml FDA standard, results can be seen in Table 1 (BG) and Table 1 (cat). (Table presented) Conclusion: Diagnostic extracts of BG used in Europe and Mexico are less potent than those used in US. As a consequence people with low BG sensitivity might give a positive SPT in US. For cat only some extracts are low potency. A similar comparison using therapeutic extracts for immunotherapy may yield important information.

In 41 patients the procedure is continuing already the third preseason/ season, the efficacy and the drug consumption was assessed before SLIT and at the beginning of the 3 year. Methods: Forty-one patients with intermittent allergic rhinoconjunctivitis and mean age was 36 years, were clinically assessed for their symptoms after the first and before the third season of SLIT by Staloral 300. Symptom score was determined according to the intensity of symptoms as: mild = 1, slight/moderate = 2, moderate = 3, severe = 4. Patients' reports on subjective well-being after two seasons and reports on drug usage were also analysed before 1th SLIT season and in the January 2010. The percentage of cases with improvement is presented separately for specific allergens: grasses, birch, trees, grasses + trees and one case of Salix. The introduction of SLIT was each year as the application of 1 to 8 drops in 90 min. The patient applied 4 drops/day sublingual and contacted us, weekly the first 2 weeks, then monthly, at the end of the season and at the 3th seasonal start. The duration of SLIT was 4 months. The symptom-score and drug consumption were summarised at start of 3. SLIT season. Results: Clinical symptom score was improved including also less or even none pharmacotherapy needed. In January 2010 the summarised improvement of symptoms/less pharmacotherapy was as follows: at grasses 86%, birch 76%, grasses + trees 48%. The case with salix on SLIT improved for 56%. All patients wanted to continue SLIT. Conclusion: Seasonal SLIT in pollen caused rhinoconjunctivitis is significant effective already in the first season, but more better in the second one. Less pharmacotherapy is needed the hole year. The best results are achieved by grass allergen and the worse by combination of two allergens. So the single proven actual allergen SLIT should be suggested. SLIT is a safe and an effective seasonal therapy.
A prospective Italian survey on the safety of short term specific immunotherapy with pollen allergoids adjuvanted by monophosphoryl lipid A (uSCIT-MPL); Background: The clinical efficacy of allergen specific immunotherapy in the treatment of allergic respiratory diseases is well documented. However its main possible drawbacks are the risk of systemic reactions and the problems of adherence, partially due to the long duration of the treatment. A recently developed immunotherapy with pollen allergoids adjuvanted by monophosphoryl lipid A requires an ultrashort pre-seasonal schedule, with only four injections (uSCIT-MPL-4). However the safety of this regimen has not been formally assessed in real life by post-marketing surveillance. Objective: To prospectively assess the safety of uSCIT-MPL-4 in a 3-year, multi-centre, real-life study. Methods: Five Italian allergy units were asked to record the clinical features of systemic reactions due to uSCIT-MPL-4. Vaccines were prescribed according to the international guidelines. Systemic reactions (SR) were graded according to the EAACI recommendations and were classified as immediate (<30 min) or delayed (>30 min). Results: A total of 510 patients (276 male, age range 6-66 years) received uSCIT-MPL-4 as follows:, 61% grass, 35.7% birch, 13.2% parietaria and 3% other pollens (ragweed, artemisia and olea). 18% of subjects were treated with more than one extract. A total of 3.308 injections were given and the mean duration of uSCIT-MPL-4 was 2, 3 years. Overall, 7 SR were observed in 510 patients (1.37%) and 2.11/ 1000 injections. All SR were delayed. Two patients with SRs discontinued uSCIT-MPL-4, whereas the remaining five patients completed the treatment, with a schedule modification. Details about these SR are shown in the Table 1. Conclusions: The rate of systemic reactions in this prospective study was very low, confirming that uSCIT-MPL-4 is a safe treatment with an acceptable risk/benefit ratio, when prescribed an carried out according to recommendations.
The clinical development of specific immunotherapies: Specific methodological issues and clinical interpretation of results; Background: Historically, the safety and efficacy of specific immunotherapy (SIT) has been demonstrated in (mainly small-scale) studies and confirmed in meta-analyses. However, the inherent sources of heterogeneity (patient selection outside the pollen season, pollen count variations, long evaluation periods) observed in recent, large-scale studies of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets mean that highly susceptible patients may not exhibit uniformly a sufficient level of symptoms during the study period to assess the efficacy of SIT. Methods: We performed randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational clinical trials of a 300IR pre- and co-seasonally administered 5-grass pollen SLIT tablet in adults and children with allergic rhinitis. The primary efficacy criterion was the mean average rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (ARTSS) over the pollen season, during which daily grass pollen counts were measured locally. To evaluate the potential relationship between disease severity and the treatment effect, investigating centres were divided in tiertiles according to their mean placebo group ARTSS. Results: Pre-seasonal inclusion of patients on the basis of retrospectively severe symptoms in the previous pollen season did not produce such a severely affected population in the study season. The apparent treatment effect of SLIT tablet was partially masked by the highly variable severity of symptoms during the whole pollen season (mean ARTSS in the adult placebo group: 4.93 ± 3.229). For the adult trial, the mean active versus placebo ARTSSs and the relative difference versus placebo (%) were 15%, 26% and 37% for the low, moderate- and high-disease severity tiertiles, respectively. In the paediatric trial, these values were 10%, 33% and 34%, respectively. Linear regression of individual daily RTSS scores and pollen counts in active and placebo groups also showed that the more severe the disease, the greater the treatment effect of SLIT tablet. Conclusion: Inherent sources of heterogeneity must be taken into account when interpreting the results of natural-exposure immunotherapy trials but none obscured the statistically significant treatment effect of SLIT. In a subgroup analysis, SLIT tablets' beneficial effect increased with disease severity.

A randomised, parallel-group, phase IV, open trial evaluating compliance to the treatment with Grazax allergen immunotherapy tablet in patients with seasonal grass pollen rhinoconjuntivitis; Background: Immunotherapy is considered the only causal treatment of respiratory allergy. Recently Allergen Immunotherapy tablet (AIT) has shown to be very effective in the treatment of grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Study aim: To evaluate the clinical effect of treatment with Grazax tablet (AIT: Allergen Immunotherapy tablet) on symptom score, and patient's acceptance in comparison with previous pollen seasons in adult subjects with grass pollen induced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Patients and Methods: A total of 261 patients suffering from grass induced mild to moderate rhinoconjuntivitis were enrolled in a multicentre study. The mean age was 32.8 ± 10 years. Men were 149 (57%) and women 112 (43%). A total of 50 subjects suffered from mild asthma (Step:I-III GINA Classification). Efficacy was evaluated after 48 weeks of treatment with Grazax tablets the impact on quality of life, symptom score, and patient's acceptance in comparison with previous pollen seasons. This was evaluated, globally, trough a 10-cm VAS scale (0 = big improvement, 5 = not improvement, 10 = worsening of symptoms). Results: A total of 81% of patients reported an improvement of symptoms after treatment with Grazax, evaluated through a VAS in comparison with the previous season. Investigators evaluated the efficacy of treatment good or very good in 85% of patients. No SAE or SU-SAR were reported in this study. Conclusion: Efficacy of treatment good or very good in 85% of patients. This is a strong indication that treatment with Grazax AIT is effective in relieving these symptoms, and it is in line with the results from previous Grazax trials.
Long-lasting clinical efficacy of allergen specific immunotherapy in adults; Background: Many controlled studies have demonstrated that allergen immunotherapy is the unique specific and effective treatment of allergic rhinitis (AR) and/or asthma. However, only limited knowledge exists about the long-term clinical efficacy of this therapy. Aim: This study was designed as retrospective controlled observational trial. Patients with AR and/or asthma treated with conventional immunotherapy between 1992 and 2000 years and those completing the previous SIT at least 5 years ago were included into the study. The control group composed of patients not receiving SIT during the same period. The two groups were well matched in terms of age, onset of disease and severity, and allergen sensitivity. Patients who had eligible medical records were invited for assessment in 2007 in terms of their symptoms, drug intake, skin test and non-specific bronchial reactivity since the end of the previous SIT in 2000. SIT and control groups were comparatively evaluated regarding at the beginning (T0), end of the SIT (T1) and the current status (T2). Results: Out of 154 patients, 30 SIT (F/M: 21/9, mean age: 30 ± 7.4 years) and 26 control group (F/M: 19/7, mean age: 31.3 ± 7.2 years) provided inclusion criteria. They were re-evaluated for a time period (mean 12.1 ± 2.5 years) including duration of SIT (4.5 ± 0.9 years) after T0 time point. Rhinitis, asthma and medication scores were significantly reduced at T2 compared to T0 and T1 (P = 0.000). Duration of SIT for a longer periods was found to be only independent factor affecting good clinical response. Twenty-two (39.2%) of a total 56 patients developed new sensitizations according to skin prick tests regardless of the groups (P = 0.278). However, the rate of 'symptomatic sensitization' among them was significantly higher in the control group (23.1%) than in the SIT group (3.3%) (P = 0.041). There was a significant decrease in skin test reactivity against grass pollen antigens, and the positivity of methacholine bronchial challenge test between T0 and T2 in the SIT group (P = 0.016). No significant change was observed in lung function parameters as well as specific and total IgE levels. Conclusion: Our study indicates that there is still an important clinical benefit average 7 years after discontinuation of SIT in adults. A striking finding of this study was not prevented development of new sensitization by the SIT. Neverthless, it seems that SIT may play a suppressive role in the onset of overt clinical symptoms.
Comparison of clinical efficacy and preventive role between subcutaneous and sublingual immunotherapy in children with seasonal allergic rhinitis; Background: Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is the most relevant alternative to the well-established subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). However, few studies directly compare the effectiveness of SLIT versus SCIT. Objective: To compare the clinical efficacy and preventive role of SLIT versus SCIT in Kuwaiti schoolchildren with seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR). Methods: Eighty-two children (mean age 14.2 years) with SAR due to sensitization to local pollen allergens (Bermuda grass and /or Salsola kali) and who fulfill inclusion criteria, participated in this single-blinded study. Patients were randomly selected (1:1) to receive either SLIT (n = 38) or SCIT (n = 44), Stallergenes France, for 3 years course. Twenty-five patients of SLIT group and 34 from SCIT group who completed 3 years treatment were evaluated for clinical efficacy (clinical symptoms score in a diary card), development of asthma, and new sensitization. Results were compared between the groups. Results: There was no significant difference between SLIT and SCIT group in terms of total clinical score and development of new sensitization, (P = 0.05 and P = 0.2, respectively). However, asthma development was significantly less among the SCIT group (P < 0.05). Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that SLIT is a promising immunotherapy. Further studies are needed for accurate assessment of SLIT, especially in children.

Tolerability of a sublingual immunotherapy preparation with an increased allergen concentration - A non-interventional observational study; Background: The tolerability of sublingual specific immunotherapy is known to be influenced by the dose of the allergen that is applied. Aim of our study was to analyse data about the tolerability of a sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) preparation with an increased allergen concentration during routine application in the allergist's office. Methods: In a non-interventional observational study, data for tolerability of SLIT with pollen and perennial allergens were recorded for the first intake under supervision by the physician and the first 14 days of therapy according to patients' diaries. As SLIT preparations, products for several allergens with increased allergen content were applied (SLITonePLUS®, mono doses, 500 STU, daily intake without updosing). All adverse drug reactions (ADR) reported were coded according to MedDRA. Results: In total, data for 452 patients with rhinoconjunctivitis (30.8% with asthma) aged 3-77 years (median 27.0) were documented by 99 practising allergists regarding the first intake of SLIT (grass mix + rye, Timothy grass, tree mix, birch, mugwort, house dust mites, cat, Alternaria). The most frequently applied allergens were grass mix + rye (135 patients), tree mix (birch/alder/hazel, 124 patients) and house dust mites (113 patients). No serious ADR were observed. ADR after the first intake of SLIT were reported in 146/452 (32.3%) patients with lower rates of ADR for patients treated with perennial allergens (27.3%) compared with grass pollen products (32.2%). ADR were predominantly reported as oral paraesthesia, oral pruritus and throat irritation and with mild severity. Overall tolerability was assessed as very good or good by 94.6% of the physicians, by 3.2% as moderate and by 2.3% as poor. Conclusion: Our study showed that a higher dose SLIT product applied daily by mono doses (SLITonePLUS®) is well tolerated for pollen and perennial allergens during the first intake and the consecutive 14 days of treatment and can, therefore, be prescribed for home treatment.
Compliance side effects and safety of rush sublingual immunotherapy with monomeric allergoid tablets; Background: Sublingual immunotherapy with monomeric allergoid tablets has been introduced 15 years ago. A large use of SLIT reduce the initiation treatment. In this assay we evaluate the compliance, side effects and safety of a rush protocol attaining the maximal dose on the fourth day. Material and methods: Fifty-eight patients aged 5-50 years (30 males, 28 females) have been included in the trial. 36 (18M, 18F) were allergic to house dust mites (Dpteronyssius, D. farinae) 16 (8M, 8F) to grass pollens and 6 (4M, 2F) to Parietaria judaica (Pellitory wall) as shown by clinical history positive skin prick tests and specific IgE to relevant allergens has been done with monomeric allergoid tablets standardized at 1000 UA units (Lofarma Laboratories, Milano, Italy) D. pteronyssius, D. farinae, Grass mix 3, Parietaria mix. The use of tablets and protocol have been carefully explained to all patients and informed consent obtained. A build-up schedule in four days has been applied. 500 UA once a day, 1000 UA, 1500 and 2000 twice a day. Afterwards a weekly dosage of 2000 UA once a day continued. During pollen season for Grass and Parietaria the dosage has been reevaluated. A diary card has been fulfilled, side effects registered. Opinion of practicability and simplicity of administration have been noted. Results: The rush protocol has been well tolerated in all 58 patients. Side effects only in 5 (8.6%) patients slight, well tolerated, during the third fourth days of buildup. Local irritation and itching in all five patients, slight self-resolving urticaria in 2 (3.4%). In four patients the side effects disappear with the progression of immunotherapy. No systemic side effects. In one patient allergic to grass pollen the dosage has to be reduced to 500 UA weekly during pollen season and 1000 UA weekly outside pollen season. All the patients complied with the protocol maintaining the weekly sublingual tablets during all the observation period. Fifty patients (86.2%) preferred the tablets to SCIT or other sublingual method (drops). Conclusions: A rush protocol with monomeric allergoid tablets can be safely applied to respiratory allergy. Side effects are very limited without any severe reactions even during pollen season. Tablets immunotherapy is well accepted by the patients and the weekly regimen helps to achieve a very large compliance. Considering the safety degree obtained a shorter protocol with a single day built-up or even a single dose protocol can be considered.

Tolerability, safety and compliance of rush sublingual immunotherapy with monomeric allergoid tablets; Background: The experience of the last years with SLIT has led to progressively reduce the duration of the up-dosing, starting sometimes already with the maintenance dose. These data suggest the possibility to shorten the initial therapy. Aim of this study was to evaluate the compliance and the safety of a new rush protocol with monomeric allergoid in tablets (allergoid SLIT, Lofarma, Milan, Italy). Method: Fifty-eight patients aged 5-50 years (28 females) were included in the trial. Thirty-six were allergic to house dust mites 16 to grass and six to Parietaria as shown by clinical history, skin prick tests and specific IgE (Phadia, Uppsala, Sweden). Both allergoid SLIT and the rush protocol were carefully explained to all patients and an informed consent was obtained. A build-up schedule lasting four days was applied: 500 AU the first day, 1000 AU the second, 1500 AU the third and 2000 AU the fourth. Tablets were given once or twice a day. The maintenance dosage of 2000 AU was started after the fourth day. During pollen season for grass and Parietaria the dosage has been re-evaluated in all the 22 patients. A diary card had to be fulfilled by each patient. An opinion about the practicability and the simplicity of the administration was asked to each patient. Results: Mild adverse reactions (ARs) were observed during the up-dosing in five patients (8.6%). They were: local irritation and itching in five and slight self-resolving urticaria in 2 (3.4%). Peach anaphylaxis due to a protein different than LTP; Background: Pru p 3, a non-specific lipid transfer protein (nsLTP), is the major allergen implicated in peach allergy in Southern Europe. Disease-modifying effect of the SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet is sustained 2 years after treatment; Background: The sustained efficacy following completion of 3 years of treatment with the SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense 75 000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK, Hørsholm, Denmark) was investigated in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III trial. Methods: The analysis set included 241 subjects (137 active and 104 placebo, providing diary data during the season). The reduction in rhinoconjunctivitis medication score was in favour of active treatment, yet not significant (median reduction 21%, mean reduction 20%, P = 0.114). ▼Grazax for hay fever - What's new?; In 2008, we reviewed Grazax, a sublingual tablet containing standardised allergen extract of grass pollen.1 At the time, this product was licensed for the treatment of adults with proven grass-pollen-induced rhinitis and conjunctivitis (hay fever). However, we were not convinced that the effect on rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores in published trials was clinically relevant. Also, given that no published studies had compared Grazax with symptomatic therapies or subcutaneous immunotherapy for hay fever, it was expensive and its long-term efficacy and safety were not known, we could not recommend its use.1 Since our review, the terms of the marketing authorisation for Grazax have been changed, such that it is now described in the summary of product characteristics (SPC) as a "disease-modifying treatment", and the drug is now also licensed for use in children aged 5 years and above.2 Here we assess the latest evidence for Grazax and reconsider the drug's place in the management of patients with hay fever.

Mimotope vaccination for therapy of allergic asthma: Anti-inflammatory effects in a mouse model; Background: One of the concerns of allergen-specific immunotherapy is the possible boost of inflammatory allergen-specific T lymphocytes. Allergen immunotherapy; Specific immunotherapy (SIT) involves the administration of allergen extracts to achieve clinical tolerance of those allergens that cause symptoms in patients with allergic conditions. Immunotherapy is effective in patients with mild forms of allergic disease and also in those who do not respond well to standard drug therapy. Most SIT is given by means of injection, but there is increasing interest in performing SIT through the sublingual route. SIT remains the treatment of choice for patients with systemic allergic reactions to wasp and bee stings and should be considered as an option in patients with allergic rhinitis, asthma, or both. SIT can modify the course of allergic disease by reducing the risk of new allergic sensitizations and inhibiting the development of clinical asthma in children treated for allergic rhinitis. The precise mechanisms responsible for the beneficial effects of SIT remain a matter of research and debate. An effect on regulatory T cells seems most probable and is associated with switching of allergen-specific B cells toward IgG4 production. Few direct comparisons of SIT and drug therapy have been made. Existing data suggest that the effects of SIT take longer to develop, but once established, SIT achieves long-lasting relief of allergic symptoms, whereas the benefits of drugs only last as long as they are continued. © 2010 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.

Clinical parameters to evaluate the efficacy of allergen-specific immunotherapy in allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Calculation of "well days" as an adjunct concept; Efficacy monitoring of immunotherapy (IT) is performed to adjust the therapy according to the patients reactions, to collect data for scientific studies and to evaluate the efficacy of IT. A decrease of allergy symptoms and of drug use are the main efficacy parameters obtained by using the symptom-medication-score (SMS). For this, allergy diaries, skin tests and nasal provocation testing are most suitable. During the period of documentation pollen exposition should be monitored with Burkhard traps. In cytologic measures specific cell activation markers and specific lymphokine-profiles can be evaluated. For the reason of their expense, those methods are restricted to scientific investigations and only rarely for routine diagnostics. Numerous clinical trials have investigated the efficacy and safety of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) using symptom- and medication-scores. The results suggest that high allergen doses are necessary to achieve adequate efficacy. An alternative approach to assess the outcome of allergen-specific immunotherapy was investigated by a new high-dose sublingual 6-grass pollen preparation. This sublingual immunotherapy significantly improved the symptom-medication-score (SMS) in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by counting "well days" (days without intake of any rescue medication and a reduction of the symptom-score) during the grass pollen season. This post-hoc analysis showed that SLIT for 1.5 years resulted in a significantly higher number of "well days" than with placebo. These results reflect the high improvement in symptom-medication-score. "Well days" can therefore be regarded as a further variable to measure efficacy of allergen-specific immunotherapy. © 2010 Dustri-Verlag Dr. Karl Feistle.
