Efficacy of non-modified allergen products for subcutaneous specific immunotherapy - Evaluation of evidence in clinical trials; Background: Allergen products for specific immunotherapy (SIT) differ in terms of qualitative and quantitative composition, standardization, application and dosage. Systematic reviews demonstrate significant heterogeneity in primary outcome of SIT studies. To ensure that patients are treated based on scientific evidence, clinical efficacy of each allergen product should be demonstrated by adequate clinical trials. Objective: To evaluate the clinical efficacy of non-modified allergen products for subcutaneous specific immunotherapy obtainable in Germany by using the recommendations for clinical trials of the World Allergy Organization (WAO). Methods: A systematic literature search was performed to identify randomized clinical trials including outcome measurement of symptom-and medication scores. Results: A total of 65 publications were identified for further analysis. 15 doubleblind, placebo-controlled (DBPC) studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were analyzed in detail. Clinical efficacy was documented for grass pollen allergic adults and children in 7 studies with 3 products and for tree pollen allergic adults in 4 studies with 3 products. In 4 studies, clinical efficacy was demonstrated in mite-allergic patients with one product. One product also showed long-term efficacy in grass allergic patients and demonstrated clinical efficacy in adults as well as in children, both, suffering from rhinoconjunctivitis and/or asthma bronchiale. In addition, secondary preventive aspects have been shown for one product in randomized trials. Conclusion: Evidence of clinical efficacy, analyzed according to the WAO recommendations for clinical SIT trials, has been demonstrated for 3 nonmodified products with 3 homologous allergen groups in 15 clinical studies. © 2010 Dustri-Verlag Dr. Karl Feistle.
Safety of anti-IgE treatment with omalizumab in children with seasonal allergic rhinitis undergoing specific immunotherapy simultaneously.; Seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) affects at least 10-25% of the Caucasian race and about 40% of patients are children. Standard treatment of SAR is specific immunotherapy (SIT), but anti-allergic drugs can significantly enhance efficacy of SIT. One candidate is the humanized monoclonal anti-IgE antibody omalizumab. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre trial in Germany. A total of 221 children were randomly assigned to four different groups and treated with SIT (either grass or birch pollen), starting at least 14 wk before the local birch pollen season. After the 12-wk SIT titration phase, either anti-IgE (omalizumab) or placebo (NaCl 0.9%) therapy was added. This combination therapy with SIT and anti-IgE or placebo lasted 24 wk. To record local reactions and adverse events (AE), the injection site was examined by a clinician 20 min after application of study medication. Further, patients stated any AE and the use of rescue medication by means of a diary 3 days after every injection. Finally, any AE or serious adverse event (SAE) reported by the patients was specified on a standard form by clinicians. Overall tolerance was judged by the doctors according to the patient's diaries. To test differences between the groups, we used either the two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test or the two-sided chi-square test. Tolerability of SIT and omalizumab treatment was good (82% of patients). Only some AE with possible causal relationship to treatment occurred slightly more often in the verum groups, i.e. local reactions (16.8 vs. 12.3%) and gastrointestinal (2.7 vs. 0.9%) and ear symptoms (1.8 vs. 0%). Most AE (93.4% in omalizumab and 87.2% in placebo group) were judged by the patients as mild to moderate. SAE were restricted to four patients with asthma in the placebo group, two subjects with headache in the verum group and three patients with infections (two in verum and one in placebo group). Only the cases of asthma were judged to be possibly related to study medication. Further, redness and swelling at the SIT injection site appeared significantly more often in the placebo group which suggests a positive effect of omalizumab on local reaction induced by SIT. Omalizumab represents an important clinical advance in the management of allergic diseases and can be considered to be safe in children. © 2009 John Wiley & Sons A/S.
Pre-seasonal specific short-term immunotherapy versus placebo in seasonal rhino-conjunctivitis; Aim: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of five years' pre-seasonal specific immunotherapy (SIT) with grass pollens versus placebo in a blind controlled study in patients with seasonal rhino-conjunctivitis. Method: The study had three stages: the pre--treatment period, SIT for two years and SIT for a further three years. Thirty-six patients were selected from a group of 60 with persistent moderate rhino-conjunctivitis (ARIA definition) sensitised to grass pollens. Eighteen patients were male (50.0%) and 18 were female (50.0%) and their mean age was 26.1 years. For five years, the patients received pre-seasonal SIT with extracts of seven grass pollens (ALK-Abello, Spain) administered in seven subcutaneous injections, with a total annual dose of 2251 SE (standardised extract). The placebo group received saline solution daily in sublingual drops for seven weeks pre-Spring. All patients received information on weather forecasts and total pollens count in their residential area via e-mail or SMS. We used the SPSS version 12 statistical software program. The ANOVA test and student's t test were used to analyse differences in symptoms and medication use between groups and the Spearman method was used to analyse correlations. Results: A significant improvement (p < 0.01) was observed in symptoms and use of medication in the SIT group (mean 23.5 days), compared with the placebo group (mean 61.9 days). The tolerance and safety of SIT were excellent. Only 0.8% of the 252 SIT injections caused local reactions. Conclusion: Subcutaneous SIT for patients sensitised to grass pollens is effective and safe. A considerable reduction in symptoms and in medication was found. Information on weather conditions and pollen count was also useful in providing nasal pollinosis patients with a better quality of life.

Immunomodulatory nanoparticles as adjuvants and allergen-delivery system to human dendritic cells: Implications for specific immunotherapy; Novel adjuvants and antigen-delivery systems with immunomodulatory properties that shift the allergenic Th2 response towards a Th1 or regulatory T cell response are desired for allergen-specific immunotherapy. This study demonstrates that 200-nm sized biodegradable poly(γ-glutamic acid) (γ-PGA) nanoparticles (NPs) are activators of human monocyte-derived dendritic cells (MoDCs). γ-PGA NPs are efficiently internalized by immature MoDCs and strongly stimulate production of chemokines and inflammatory cytokines as well as up-regulation of co-stimulatory molecules and immunomodulatory mediators involved in efficient T cell priming. Furthermore, MoDCs from allergic subjects stimulated in vitro with a mixture of γ-PGA NPs and extract of grass pollen allergen Phleum pratense (Phl p) augment allergen-specific IL-10 production and proliferation of autologous CD4+ memory T cells. Thus, γ-PGA NPs are promising as sophisticated adjuvants and allergen-delivery systems in allergen-specific immunotherapy. © 2010 Elsevier Ltd.

Treatment with the SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet in children above and below the age of 10 - Efficacy, safety and immunological response; Purpose: Treatment with the SQ-standardised grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), GRAZAX® (Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK, Denmark), is efficacious and well-tolerated in grass allergic patients. Younger children are often perceived as good candidates for immunotherapy, and post-hoc analyses to explore possible differences between younger and older children were performed for a grass AIT paediatric phase III trial. Methods: Of 253 children aged 5-16 years with grass allergy were randomised 1:1 to receive grass AIT or placebo prior to and during the grass pollen season 2007. Symptomatic medications were provided as rescue medication to both groups. The population was divided into two age groups comprising 140 children aged 5-10 years and 113 children aged 11-16 years. The effect of age on efficacy was also analysed by including age as a covariate in the symptom score analysis. Results: Analysis of the difference between active and placebo for each age group showed a slightly higher relative difference in symptom score for the younger children compared with the older, 26% versus 19%. The difference between active and placebo was statistically significant for the 5-10 year-olds (P = 0.047), although the trial was powered for analysis of the population as a whole. Including age as a covariate in the symptom score analysis indicated age to have no influence on the efficacy, as demonstrated by a p-value of 0.6 for the interaction between age and treatment. In the AIT group the percentage of adverse events assessed as treatment-related was nominally lower for the younger group than for the older, 32% versus 40%. The percentages of adverse events assessed as moderate or severe in the active group were similar for the two age groups. For both active and placebo, the overall number of adverse events was higher in the younger group than in the group of older children. The immunological response (IgE, IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor) was similar for the two age groups. There was a tendency for the younger group towards an increased response in IgE-blocking factor at the onset of the grass pollen season, both in the active and the placebo group. Conclusions: The phase III trial, investigating the SQ-standardised grass AIT, demonstrated once-daily administration to be clinically efficacious and well-tolerated in children between 5 and 16 years. Comparison of two age groups revealed similar efficacy and tolerability after treatment with grass AIT independent of age.

Sustained, disease-modifying effect of grass allergy tablet immunotherapy 1 year after a 3-year treatment period; Background: The sustained efficacy with the SQ-standardised grass allergy immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax® (Phleum pratense 75,000 SQ-T, ALK-Abello, Denmark), 1 year after a 3-year treatment period, was investigated in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase III trial. Participants were adults with a history of moderate to severe grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis inadequately controlled by symptomatic medications. Methods: The full analysis set included 283 participants (157 AIT, 126 placebo). All participants had free access to symptomatic medications during the grass pollen season. Primary and key secondary efficacy endpoints were rhinoconjunctivitis symptom and medication scores, quality of life, and percentages of symptom and medication free days. Immunological endpoints included specific IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor. Safety was assessed by adverse events. Results: 1 year after treatment, the grass AIT group showed a 26% reduction in mean rhinoconjunctivitis symptom scores (P < 0.001) and a 29% reduction in medication scores (P = 0.022) when compared with placebo. The corresponding median reductions were 31% and 52%. This level of efficacy was similar to the efficacy during treatment. The mean difference in percentages of symptom and medication free days during the entire season was 27% (P= 0.038) (median difference 49%) in favour of AIT. The grass AIT group also reported better rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life (P= 0.004). No safety issues were identified. Conclusion: Significant and clinically relevant efficacy of grass AIT was sustained 1 year after a 3-year treatment period. This is the first time evidence of disease modification by sublingual tablet immunotherapy has been demonstrated in a large-scale, randomised, placebo-controlled trial.

Rationale for five-grass pollen vaccine; Grass pollen. allergic patients are naturally exposed and sensitized to multiple pollens from various Pooideae species. The question arises as to whether such patients should be desensitized with extracts based on a single pollen or a pollen mixture. Neither conventional diagnosis based on IgE reactivity nor pollen counts enable the identification of which grass species are involved in patient sensitization. Significant cross-immunogenicity is observed between allergens from Pooideae pollens due to their conserved amino acid sequences (e.g. > 90% for group 1, 55-80% for group 5, 30-60% for other allergens, including minor allergens). Nevertheless, pollen allergens also contain species-specific T or B cell epitopes, and there is evidence that at least 50% of allergic patients are sensitized to such distinct epitopes. In addition, substantial quantitative differences exist in the allergen (e.g. group 1, 2/3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 13) content of pollens obtained from distinct grass species. In this context, we recommend a vaccine consisting of a combination of pollens from five common and well characterized Pooideae including Anthoxanthum odoratum, Dactylis glomerata, Lolium perenne, Phleum pratense and Poa pratensis for desensitization purposes. This 5-grass mixture is recommended because, (i) it has been validated, in terms of safety and efficacy, by established clinical practice

A contemporary review of sublingual immunotherapy; The sublingual route has become an interesting and novel therapeutic option for the immunotherapeutic management of patients with allergies. Immunotherapy modifies the immune response by decreasing the specific IgE levels and Th2-type inflammation in the mucosa when allergen exposure occurs, shifting this toward a Th1-type response. Credible evidence exists of both effectiveness and safety of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) from several placebo-controlled double-blind studies. SLIT has been shown to be an effective treatment of allergic rhinitis and asthma in both children and adults. The therapy is well tolerated with mainly minor gastrointestinal side effects that subside in few weeks. The ideal treatment length and dosage still require further verification. Additional studies evaluating long-term efficacy and the immune response of SLIT still need to be performed, and additional standardized antigens still need to be developed. © 2009 The American Laryngological, Rhinological and Otological Society, Inc.

Temperature stabilitv and mixing compaitbilitv of phenolated, glycerinated short ragweed extracts; Introduction: Glycerinated short ragweed extracts are incorporated into immunotherapy regimens with increasing frequency due to their improved stability compared to aqueous products. The inclusion of phenol as an anti-bacterial preservative in these products is believed by some clinicians to reduce ragweed (and other) allergen activities. However, little data is available to support these claims in ragweed extracts alone or in extract mixtures typically used for immunotherapy. Methods: In this study, the stabilities and compatibilities of phenolated (0.2%), glycerinated (50%) short ragweed extracts were assessed after storage at moderate temperatures (20-40 deg C) or after mixing with a variety of high-protease (fungal, insect) and low-protease (grass pollen, cat, dust mite) allergens. Test samples and controls contained equivalent phenol and glycerin levels, and were analyzed by short ragweed-specific Amb a 1 radial immunodiffusion assays using the identical reagents distributed by FDA for ragweed extract standardization. Results: Short ragweed extracts at various concentrations or mixtures of short ragweed and low-protease or insect products exhibited no major changes in Amb a 1 concentrations after storage at ambient temperatures (20-25 deg C) for up to 12 months. Short ragweed extracts mixed with fungal products and stored under the same conditions resulted in Amb a 1 recoveries ranging from 58% (Penicillium) to 84% (Aspergillus). Exposure of short ragweed extract concentrates to higher temperatures (30-40 deg C) for up to 3 months reduced Amb a 1 levels by approximately 10% per month. The high levels of Amb a 1 stability observed across 11 different short ragweed solutions examined in these studies demonstrated that phenol exerted very little (if any) degradative effects on this major allergen. Conclusions: Phenolated, glycerinated short ragweed extracts retained high levels of Amb a 1 activity after storage at moderate temperatures or mixing with other extract concentrates, conditions known to compromise aqueous short ragweed allergens or mixtures. Only exposure to elevated temperature (40 deg C) or combination with certain fungal extracts produced noticeable changes in Amb a 1 levels. All recoveries exceeded 50% of initial Amb a 1 values, supporting the use of these solutions in a wide variety of immunotherapy procedures.

The SQ-standardized grass allergy immunotherapy tabletis well tolerated over 3 years of treatment; Introduction: Traditionally, allergen-specific immunotherapy has been administered via subcutaneous injections or sublingual drops. Recently, a new formulation administered sublingually, allergy immunotherapy tablets (AIT), has emerged. Many large double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials have demonstrated AIT to be well tolerated and efficacious in reducing rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms and the use of rescue medications. We investigated the nature, severity and duration of the most common adverse events (AEs) associated with treatment with an SQ-standardized grass AIT (Phleum pratense, 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU, ALK, Denmark) during a trial conducted over a 3 year period. Methods: Subjects with grass-allergy (n=634) were enrolled in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial, of which 351 continued in a 2-year extension. Approval was obtained from the local IRBs and written informed consent obtained from all subjects. Subjects were randomized 1:1 to grass AIT or placebo. All AEs were collected and rated as mild, moderate or severe. AEs were assessed as treatment-emergent if the start date was on or after the date of the first tablet intake. Reactions occurring for a limited period of time each day on consecutive days were reported as one event. Results: The most frequent AEs after grass AIT were oral pruritus (164 subjects, 191 events), mouth edema (65 subjects, 70 events), ear pruritus (41 subjects, 42 events) and throat irritation (34 subjects, 37 events). The majority of these AEs were mild (84%) or moderate (13%) and transient of nature. There was a sharp decrease in the percentage of subjects reporting these AEs within the first weeks ofthe trial (figure). Approximately 10% continued to have oral itching during the entire trial, typically lasting 10 minutes after tablet administration. Withdrawal due to these local AEs was low (n=6, 1%). Conclusions: The most frequent AEs after grass AIT were local reactions affecting the mucosal membranes in mouth, ear and throat. The majority of AEs were mild and generally subsided shortly after treatment initiation, indicating development of tolerance. A small proportion of the subjects experienced local AEs daily upon tablet administration. However, the rate of withdrawals due to local AEs was low, indicating that grass AIT was well tolerated and these side effects were acceptable to most patients. (Figure Presented).
Diagnosis and management of allergic rhinitis; • Objective: To provide an overview of the approach to diagnosis and management of allergic rhinitis. • Methods: Review of the literature. • Results: Allergic rhinitis affects 20% to 40% of the U.S. population and has a significant impact on patients, their families, and society. The diagnosis can often be ascertained from a history that points to a specific, often seasonal or environmental, trigger. Treatment is often begun without the aid of any testing and based on a diagnosis made on history and physical examination alone. The mainstays of first-line treatment are nonsedating oral antihistamines, nasal corticosteroids, and nasal antihistamine sprays. As an adjunct, mast cell stabilizing antihistamine eye drops may be used. First-line pharmacotherapy should be based on the nature and severity of the patient's symptoms. Allergy testing should be considered when a patient's symptoms are not controlled by routine medical therapies. • Conclusion: Allergy is a significant burden to society. A symptom-based approach to the pharmacologic treatment of allergic rhinitis will yield the most satisfactory control of the patient's major symptoms.
The future of sublingual immunotherapy.; Sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is currently the most prescribed form of allergen immunotherapy in many European countries. Its use has been accepted in the international consensus publications, and recently also the scepticism of USA scientists is attenuated. Still, this treatment may be improved, and the possible developments consist of modification of the materials, use of adjuvants and use of recombinant allergens. Moreover, new applications of SLIT, such as food allergy, seem promising. Concerning materials, the future form of SLIT is likely to be represented by tablets, which were already tested for efficacy and safety with grass pollen extracts, and are likely to increase the convenience for the patient by the use of no-updosing schedule. Adjuvants fitting with the characteristics of SLIT seem to be CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (CpG), able to interact with the Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) whose activation induces a Th1-like pattern of cytokine release, combination of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 plus dexamethasone (VitD3-Dex), and Lactobacillus plantarum. The approach with recombinant allergens, named component-resolved diagnosis, offers the possibility to tailor immunotherapy, which was found to be effective in two randomized trials of subcutaneous SIT (16-17), while studies with SLIT are not yet available. Regarding food allergy, an important controlled study demonstrated that SLIT with hazelnut is able to increase patients tolerance over possible reactions from inadvertent assumption of the culprit food, and warrants for further trials with other foods.

Rationale for a five-grass pollen vaccine; Grass pollen allergic patients are naturally exposed and sensitized to multiple pollens from various Pooideae species. The question arises as to whether such patients should be desensitized with extracts based on a single pollen or a pollen mixture. Neither conventional diagnosis based on IgE reactivity nor pollen counts enable the identification of which grass species are involved in patient sensitization. Significant cross-immunogenicity is observed between allergens from Pooideae pollens due to their conserved amino acid sequences (e.g. >90% for group 1, 55-80% for group 5, 30-60% for other allergens, including minor allergens). Nevertheless, pollen allergens also contain species-specific T or B cell epitopes, and there is evidence that at least 50% of allergic patients are sensitized to such distinct epitopes. In addition, substantial quantitative differences exist in the allergen (e.g. group 1, 2/3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 13) content of pollens obtained from distinct grass species. In this context, we recommend a vaccine consisting of a combination of pollens from five common and well characterized Pooideae including Anthoxanthum odoratum, Dactylis glomerata, Lolium perenne, Phleum pratense and Poa pratensis for desensitization purposes. This 5-grass mixture is recommended because, (i) it has been validated, in terms of safety and efficacy, by established clinical practice
Allergenicity and cross-reactivity of pine pollen; Background Pine pollen has long been considered a non-allergenic pollen. The large size of the grain and its low levels of proteins are the main reasons invoked to explain this low allergenicity. The aim of this study was to describe the main allergenic bands of Pinus radiata (PR) and its cross-reactivity with other pine species, other conifers and grass pollen. Methods Sixty-five pine-pollen-allergic patients (51% also sensitized to grass pollen) were studied. Skin prick tests (SPT) to a battery of allergens including PR, Pinus pinea, Pinus sylvestris, Pinus nigra and Cupressus sempervirens pollens and specific IgE determination to PR and Pinus strobus were performed. IgE-immunoblotting to a PR extract and other pine pollens was also carried out. UniCAP inhibition and immunoblotting inhibition studies were performed to assess the cross-reactivity between different pollens. Results The SPTs were positive with all the pine pollen extracts tested in 69% of the patients. Specific IgE was positive to PR or P. strobus in 77% of the patients, and to Lolium perenne in 51%. Nine different allergenic bands were detected. The two main allergens were a 42 kDa band recognized by 85% of the patients and a band of approximately 6-8 kDa recognized by 40%. A high degree of cross-reactivity was observed between different pine pollen species, but not between pines and C. sempervirens pollen. A partial cross-reactivity could be seen between pine and grass pollens only in patients also sensitized to L. perenne. Conclusions Pine pollen should be considered as a potential allergenic pollen especially where this pollen is abundant. The detection of a high number of patients that were monosensitized to pine pollen suggests the possibility of treating these patients with specific immunotherapy. © 2009 Blackwell Publishing Ltd.
Efficacy of grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy for three consecutive seasons and after cessation of treatment: The ECRIT study; Background: Data supporting a carry-over effect with sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) are scarce. Recombinant allergens for following antibody-responses during immunotherapywith a grass pollen vaccine and after five years of discontinuation; Objectives: Follow-up of antibody responses in serum samples from grass pollen allergic patients having received one course of injection immunotherapy (SIT) with an aluminium hydroxide-adsorbed grass pollen extract (n=12) or only anti-inflammatory treatment (n=7). Mass spectrometric investigation of molecular variability of grass pollen group 1 allergens; Natural grass pollen allergens exhibit a wide variety of isoforms. Precise characterization of such microheterogeneity is essential to improve diagnosis and design appropriate immunotherapies. Moreover, standardization of allergen vaccine production is a prerequisite for product safety and efficiency. Both qualitative and quantitative analytical methods are thus required to monitor and control the huge natural variability of pollens, as well as final product quality. Allergic rhinitis; Childhood rhinitis may be classified into non-allergic and allergic. Allergic rhinitis is further divided into seasonal and perennial. Seasonal rhinitis is a disease particularly of teenagers and young adults and appears to be less common in primary and pre school age children. In seasonal rhinitis, with relevant grass pollen sensitization, the link between the allergen exposure and rhinitis is clear cut. However, in other situations such as perennial rhinitis and house dust mite allergen sensitization, the link between symptoms and allergen exposure is less certain. Avoidance of allergens often proves to be difficult in practice. Intranasal steroids are the treatment of choice for persistent moderate-severe allergic rhinitis and are more effective than antihistamines for relief of nasal obstruction. Antihistamines are effective for control of histamine related symptoms such as itching, rhinorrhoea and sneezing. The use and benefits of sublingual or injectable immunotherapy in children are controversial. © 2009 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

Efficacy and safety of a 300IR five-grass pollen SLIT tablet in children and adolescents with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis; Background: The efficacy and safety of a five-grass pollen 300IR sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablet (Stallergenes SA, France) has recently been confirmed in children and adolescents with grass pollen allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Secondary and complementary analyses on the trial's intention-to-treat (ITT) population were performed for the Average Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score (ARTSS), the six Average Individual Symptom Scores (AISSs) and for safety parameters according to age class (5 to 11 and 12 to 17). Methods: Two hundred and seventy-eight children (5-17 years of age) with grass pollen-related rhinoconjunctivitis were included in a multinational, randomized, doubleblind, placebo-controlled phase III trial. They were treated with once-daily five grasspollen SLIT tablets or placebo tablets 4 months prior to and then throughout the pollen season. Each symptom was evaluated daily by the patients (with parental assistance, for the youngest) on a four-point scale from 0 (absent) to 3 (severe). Results: The difference between 300IR and placebo tablets was significant for rhinorrhea (P = 0.038), nasal congestion (P = 0.0012), ocular pruritus (P < 0.0001) and watery eyes (P = 0.0008). Improvements in sneezing and nasal pruritus were not statistically significant. Patients aged 12 to 17 had higher ARTSSs and AISSs than those aged 5 to 11 years whatever the treatment group and the analysed period (pollen season or pollen peak). In both age classes (12-17 and 5-11), the ARTSS was lower in the 300IR group (3.77 and 2.94, respectively) than in the placebo group (4.98 and 4.08, respectively). A complementary subgroup analysis on safety parameters revealed a similar safety profile of the 300IR five-grass pollen sublingual tablet in age subgroups 5-11 and 12-17, as well as in sub-goups 5-7 and 8-11. Conclusion: Five-grass pollen tablet immunotherapy has a significant effect on eye and nasal symptoms such as nasal congestion and rhinorrhea and was in this study an effective treatment for grass polleninduced allergic rhinoconjunctivitis in children and adolescents, independently of age class. Also, the same dose can be administered to allergic children and adolescents aged 5-17 years without any influence on the tolerability of the treatment.
Safety and efficacy of recombinant grass pollen allergens: A dose - response study; Background: Recombinant DNA technology has delivered the prospect of a new generation of preparations for allergen-specific immunotherapy. The first clinical studies with recombinant allergens have yielded encouraging results. A cocktail of the most relevant recombinant major allergens of timothy grass (Phleum pratense) responsible for grass pollen allergy has been evaluated in a dose-response study to measure the tolerability and efficacy of four increasing doses. Methods: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-centre, phase II SCIT (subcutaneous immunotherapy) study was performed in 50 patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, with or without asthma. Stratification according to symptom severity was performed and 10 patients per arm were randomised to treatment groups to receive either maximum doses of 20 μg, 40 μg, 80 μg or 120 μg rPhleum or placebo. Thirteen injections were planned to apply in a pre-seasonal treatment scheme in weekly intervals. The primary endpoint (EP) of this study was the number of patients with at least one systemic reaction (according to Tryba Grading 1 - 4) with possible, probable or definite relationship to the study medication determined at the end of the updosing phase. Secondary EPs included specific antibody response and change in specific conjunctival and intracutaneous test with natural grass pollen Phleum allergen before and at the end of the trial. Results: Eight of 50 patients had systemic reactions according to the primary EP definition, all in patients receiving one of the 4 doses of active but with no significant differences between the 5 treatment groups (P = 0.591). In all verum groups IgG1 and IgG4 antibodies increased, while there was no increase in the placebo group. Positive effects on the conjunctival provocation test were detected in all active treatment groups. The intracutaneous test both, for early and late response, in wheal and erythema showed decreases with rising doses. Conclusion: Treatment with even very high doses of a cocktail of recombinant major allergens of timothy grass has shown to be safe and efficacious. Intracutaneous test suggest that skin reactivity decreases with rising doses. Moreover, the immunogenic activity of the active trial medication could be demonstrated by the induction or increase of allergen specific IgG1 and IgG4.
Early onset of action of a five-grass pollen 300 IR sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablet evaluated in an allergen Challenge Chamber; Background: The efficacy and safety of the 300 IR grass pollen SLIT tablet have been evaluated in clinical studies performed during the pollen season. However, no information on the onset of action of any type of SLIT has been reported. The Vienna Challenge Chamber (VCC) was developed as a pharmacodynamic assessment tool in which highly reproducible allergen challenge sessions are used to overcome problems related to pollen season unpredictability. Methods: Patients with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis were randomized into either active (300 IR SLIT tablets, od) (Oralair® Grasses Stallergenes, France) or placebo groups treated for 4 months out of the season, without rescue medication usage. A standardized grass pollen challenge (at a stable count of 1450-1500 grains per m, with symptom evaluation every 15 min) was performed at baseline and after 1 week and 1, 2 and 4 months of treatment. The primary efficacy endpoint was the active versus placebo difference in the Average Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score (ARTSS) after 4 months or at the last challenge. Allergen-specific basophil activation, T cell proliferation and plasma IgE and IgG responses were also assessed before and after 4 months of treatment. Results: In the ITT population (n = 89), a significant treatment effect was seen after the 1st month (P = 0.0042) and 2nd month (P = 0.02) of SLIT and was maintained through to month 4 (P = 0.0007). In the active group, the ARTSS decreased at each challenge, i.e. week 1 (7.40 ± 2.68), month 1 (5.89 ± 2.43), month 2 (5.09 ± 2.09) and month 4 (4.85 ± 2.0). The SLIT was well tolerated. The most frequent adverse events (>5% in at least one group) were local and as expected: oral pruritus, throat irritation and ear pruritus. Of the immunological parameters tested, only induction of allergen-specific IgGs was associated with a clinical response. Conclusion: For the first time ever, the onset of action and efficacy of Oralair®Grasses SLIT tablets have been assessed (versus placebo) in an ACC. The effect of this 300 IR grass pollen SLIT tablet on rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms was statistically significant (versus placebo) from the first month of treatment onward.

Evolution of subcutaneous specific immunotherapy formulations for seasonal allergic rhinitis; Background: The recent availability of Phase III data for ultra short course specific immunotherapy (uSCIT) for seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) to grass pollen highlights the evolution of SCIT technology from conventional allergen extracts. Here, we review literature from the past 5 years to determine the differences between standard extract SCIT and more recent formulations. Methods: Research articles on PubMed published during the last 5 years which reported clinical endpoints from SCIT regimens for SAR were selected and reviewed. SCIT formulations included allergen extracts, recombinant allergens, allergoids and adjuvanted allergoids. Results: Reduction in symptoms, medication usage or a combination of the two were commonly used as clinical outcome measures. SCIT was typically found to reduce symptoms or combined symptom/medication scores by ∼30% more than placebo and to be effective in over 80% of patients after one season of therapy. All regimens were well tolerated, and serious adverse reactions were generally rare. Fewer systemic and serious adverse reactions occurred following allergoid-based therapy compared with allergen-based preparations. The uSCIT (adjuvanted allergoid) formulation had the lowest injection burden and was one of two formulations which did not require ongoing maintenance therapy during the pollen season after the induction period. Conclusions: Developing technologies in SCIT have made this mode of therapy a more convenient and realistic option for SAR patients. The clinical efficacy of SCIT has been known for some time. However, practical restraints on its administration have made conventional SCIT relatively inconvenient. uSCIT appears to offer all of the clinical benefits of conventional SCIT but without many of the practical drawbacks, and can be given safely to appropriately-selected patients.

The novel acute adjuvant-free murine model of bronchial asthma induced by timothy pollen allergen; Background: The purpose of the study was to develop an acute mouse model of bronchial asthma (BA) based on timothy pollen allergen without adjuvant and to establish the immunological, cellular, morphological and functional airway features of this model. Methods: Timothy grass pollen extract (G6) was prepared by standard procedure (Koke solution extraction) and allergenicity as well as total protein content was characterized. Female BALB/c mice (n = 21) were immunized intraperitoneally seven times every other day with 20 mkg (in protein equivalent)/mouse G6 (experimental group). Two weeks later mice were challenged by eight daily intranasal instillations of 500 mkg/mouse G6. Control group (n = 21) was sham treated with saline. Blood sampling was prepared on day 27 and 43. Serum levels of anti-G6 IgE were detected in pooled sera of mice by passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) using rats. log2 of reciprocal titers of PCA were compared using Fox criteria. Bronchial hyperresponsiveness (BHR) to methacholine (1, 3 and 5 min after intravenous injection of 50 mkg/kg and 200 mkg/kg MCh) was measured on day 42 using pneumotachography. Forty-eight hour after last intranasal introduction blood, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and lungs were sampled for histological examinations. Results: The levels of anti-G6 IgE were significantly increased after intranasal instillations of G6 (to 1: 128 sera titer). There were marked features of allergic inflammation in BAL and lung tissue (increment of eosinophil counts, destruction and desquamation of bronchial epithelium, leukocytic peribronchial and perivascular infiltration). The pneumotachography assessment of BHR revealed statistically significant increase of relative and absolute breathing period and decrease of amplitude due to MCh intravenous injections in the model group. Conclusion: The developed acute adjuvantfree murine model is an important tool in the study of aetiopathogeny of human BA and for preclinical evaluation of antiasthmatic therapy (especially antigen-specific immunotherapy) in terms of its safety and effectiveness.
Efficacy of a rush immunotherapy with a depigmented polymerised extract of grass pollen assessed in an Environmental Challenge Chamber; Background: To avoid well known environmental exposure variations we investigated the efficacy of a quick up-titration immunotherapy with a depigmented polymerized allergen extract of grass mixture (Depiquick Grass Mix) in patients with allergic rhinitis under standardized Environmental Challenge Chamber (ECC) conditions. The present clinical study evaluated the efficacy and safety of a subcutaneous immunotherapy with Depiquick Grass Mix extract versus placebo administered in patients suffering from at least moderate response upon 4000 Dactylis glomerata pollen grains/m3 within 2 h exposure in the ECC. Methods: Patient selection: Seventy-two male and female patients aged 20-63 years with hay fever due to grass pollen sensitization were enrolled based on a mild to moderate response upon 4000 Dactylis glomerata pollen grains/m3 within 2 h in the ECC. Main exclusion criteria: Clinically significant sensitization against tree pollen, weed pollen and perennial allergens, persistent asthma (GINA ≥II). Treatment: Immunotherapy was performed using 1000 DPP/ml depigmented and polymerized allergenic extract of grass pollen. The rush treatment began with 0.2 ml followed by 0.3 ml after 30 min at day 1 followed by 5 injections of 0.5 ml/2 weeks. Placebo treatment was performed identically using Depiquick vehicle. Primary outcome was the change from baseline in the median 'Total Nasal Symptom Score' (TNSS) during the allergen challenge which consists of the 4 symptoms nasal obstruction, rhinorrhea, nasal itching, sneezing each scored on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (VAS) ranging from 'none' to 'severe'. Results: Analysis was based on the PP set (N = 69) using a nonparametric test (Median test). Median baseline TNSS for the active group was 152 and for the placebo group 159. The median pre-post difference of the TNSS was - 67 (44%) in the Depiquick Grass Mix and - 45 (28%) in the placebo group, a statistically significant difference between the groups (P = 0.04). Defining responders with an improvement of 30% in TNSS a statistical significant difference between treatment groups could be observed: 23/35 (66%) active and 13/34 (38%) placebo patients responded (P < 0.03). Eleven patients of the Depiquick Grass Mix and 10 of the placebo group developed mild systemic reactions s.a. rhinitis, conjunctivitis, headache, hoarseness and pruritus. Conclusions: Short-term rush immunotherapy with Depiquick Grass Mix was effective and safe as determined by means of ECC evaluation.

Quality of life benefits for patients with seasonal grass pollen-allergic rhinoconjunctivitis receiving ultra short course subcutaneous immunotherapy (uSCIT) with MPL adjuvant; Background: Seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis is known to affect quality of life and the ability to perform everyday tasks. This effect has been demonstrated using allergy-specific quality of life (QoL) questionnaires, which have consistently recorded lower QoL in patients with the condition than in controls. This multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled study examined the effects of ultra short course subcutaneous immunotherapy (uSCIT) with monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL) adjuvant on QoL for patients with seasonal grass pollen-allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Methods: A total of 1028 patients were randomised to receive four preseasonal injections of uSCIT with MPL adjuvant (n = 514) or placebo (n = 514). A validated rhinoconjunctivitis questionnaire (RQLQ) was used to evaluate QoL. Seven domains were assessed: activities, sleep, non-nose/eye symptoms, ocular symptoms, practical problems, nasal symptoms and emotional wellbeing. The scores were recorded when the first dose of uSCIT was administered (an assessment of the previous pollen season), 2-3 weeks after the final dose, in the middle of the grass pollen season and then again after the season (assessing the previous week). Results: As expected, in both groups, RQLQ scores were lowest at the mid-season assessment. No significant difference was demonstrated between treatment groups, pre or postseason. During the pollen season, the overall RQLQ scores for patients treated with uSCIT were significantly better than those recorded by the subjects who had received placebo (P = 0.0153). In addition to this, better scores were recorded by the uSCIT-treated group than by the placebo group during the pollen season for the individual domains of activities (P = 0.0045), nonnose/eye symptoms (P = 0.020), practical problems (P = 0.023), nasal symptoms (P = 0.053) and emotional wellbeing (n = 0.0097)

Does allergen specific immunotherapy influence clinical chemistry and haematology laboratory parameters in adults?; Background: A standard clinical variable in clinical trials with products for allergen specific immunotherapy (SIT) is the measurement of allergen specific antibody response. In addition, the upcoming European Medicines Agency (EMEA) guideline on the clinical development of products for SIT requested the performance of more general safety laboratory including haematology and blood chemistry tests. We checked laboratory variables of two clinical trials with two different routes of application of grass and birch pollen extract to address the question whether SIT has an impact on routine laboratory parameters. Methods: Thirteen haematological laboratory parameters and eight clinical chemistry parameters were evaluated from two double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, multi-centre, phase III clinical trials with 373 patients in total suffering from allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with or without asthma. The status at baseline was compared with the values obtained at the end of the double blind study phase. A sum of 162 patients were treated with a high-dose sublingual grass pollen preparation or placebo for 14 months. The other 211 patients were treated with a subcutaneous hypoallergenic birch pollen allergoid or placebo for 2 years. Gamma GT was measured only in the study with the subcutaneous hypoallergenic birch pollen preparation. Median values of each parameter from baseline and after treatment were compared. Differences in the median values of more than 10% were discussed. Results: SIT with a high-dose sublingual grass pollen preparation or a subcutaneous hypoallergenic birch pollen allergoid did not show an influence on any of the 21 laboratory parameters analysed here from two studies. Conclusion: The evaluation of these parameters during the screening-process of clinical trials is essential in view of potential contraindications. The need for repeated measurement of these parameters after SIT routinely in each clinical trial during the development process may be subject of consideration, at least for preparation from natural sources as evaluated here.
Grass allergen tablet immunotherapy in children induces IgG4 antibody and 4IgE-blocking responses similar to those seen in adults; Background: Serum antibody responses were investigated after ALK grass allergen tablet immunotherapy (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense 75 000 SQ-T/2800 BAU, ALK-Abelló) in children and results compared to those obtained after the same treatment in adults. Methods: In randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multi-centre trials in children (5-16 year) and adults (18-65 year), AIT was initiated prior to the grass pollen season, and once-daily treatment was continued until the end of the season. All participants had a clinical history of moderate to severe grass allergy. The levels of Phleum pratense specific IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor (i.e. serum components competing with IgE for allergen binding) were assessed in serum samples before, during and after the grass pollen season. Results: In children, specific IgG4 was significantly increased from the initial level at all assessments after treatment initiation in the active group (P < 0.001). The increase after 7.3 months of treatment was 32 U/l. In adults, 8 months of treatment led to an increase in the active group of 45.7 U/l from the initial level (P < 0.001). The IgE-blocking factor increased in the active AIT groups in both children and adults (significantly different treatment effect in the active groups compared to the placebo groups, P < 0.001 in both trials). In children the difference from the initial level in IgE-blocking factor in the active group was 0.25 after 7.3 months, while in adults the difference was 0.15 after 8 months. The adult placebo group showed no significant change while the paediatric placebo group showed a slight increase in IgE-blocking factor during the grass pollen season. The clinical treatment effect in children by means of the rhinoconjunctivitis symptom score and the percentage of well days was also similar to that observed in adults when looking at comparable pollen exposure periods. Conclusion: These data confirm comparable elevations in serum IgG4 antibodies and IgE-blocking activity in children compared with adults following successful treatment with ALK grass AIT. In addition, the higher seasonal elevations in IgE-blocking activity in placebo-treated children compared with adults, suggest that children may establish a more tolerogenic rather than allergic immune response during the grass pollen season. This observation suggests that the use of AIT in childhood may ameliorate the ongoing natural course of the disease more efficiently than AIT during adulthood.

Grass pollen preseasonal immunotherapy: The effect on direct medical cost and quality of life; Background: Preseasonal allergen specific immunotherapy (SIT) has been shown to be effective and safe in short-term. Methods: Seventy-eight adult patients with AR/asthma who live in Ankara city were included in this prospective, observational study. The first year (2007), all patients kept regularly diary cards for daily symptom and medication scores during the pollen season. At the second year (2008), they were randomly selected for SIT (n:36) and control groups (n:42). Bronchial immunotolerance after ultrashort-course immunotherapy adjuvanted with Monophosphoryl lipid a; Introduction: After several years of specific immunotherapy (SCIT) there is an increase in specific bronchial tolerance. To what extent this effect can be seen after a shortterm immunotherapy with Monophosphoryl lipid A (Pollinex Quattro®) is so far unclear. Methods: In a prospective study including 44 children double-sensitized to birch and grass pollen (33 male, average age 10.5 years) the development of bronchial tolerance before, 4 weeks after SCIT, and after the pollen season was studied. All patients received a SCIT for birch, but only those with a positive bronchial allergen challenge (drop of FEV1 >20% after inhalation of 30 AU of grass pollen) received a SCIT for grass pollen. Results: According to the result of the bronchial allergen challenge the patients were divided into three groups: Group 1: FEV1 drop <7%, n = 24, group 2: > 7 < 20%, n = 10, group 3: ≥20%, n = 10. After the pollen season group 1 worsened significantly (P < 0.01), group 2 was unchanged. Those who received immunotherapy (group 3) improved 4 weeks after SCIT (FEV1-drop 36 versus 10%, P < 0.001). This improvement in bronchial tolerance was only transient and at the end of the pollen season no longer detectable (FEV1-drop 30%, P = 0.61). Conclusion: In patients with grass pollen allergy without SCIT the specific bronchial sensitivity increased significantly. We are the first to demonstrate an increased bronchial tolerance in patients receiving SCIT 4 weeks after treatment. Unfortunately this effect was significantly weakened after the pollen season. Probably further cycles of therapy are needed for the development of a sustained bronchial tolerance.

The effect of the matched pairs method on the measurement of treatment effect in a trial of ultra short course specific immunotherapy; Background: A common problem during the assessment of specific immunotherapy (SIT) in patients with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis is incomplete data from patient diaries during the pollen season. Such data gaps may be filled using the matched pairs method, but this process has the potential to distort the data and invite misleading conclusions. Here we compare whole-population, matched-pair data from a large Phase III trial with the subgroup of patients for whom complete data were available to assess the effect of the matched pairs method. Methods: In a large, randomised, Phase III trial, 1028 patients with moderate-to-severe allergic rhinoconjunctivitis to grass pollen received ultra short course specific immunotherapy (uSCIT) or placebo. Efficacy was measured using a combined symptom and medication score (CSMS) from patient diary data collected during the four peak weeks of pollen exposure. We compared data for the whole population, which utilised a matched pairs method to fill data gaps, with data from the subset of subjects for whom complete data were available. Results: There were 343 subjects for whom 28 diary entries were available during the four peak weeks of the pollen season (177 uSCIT, 166 placebo). In both the whole population and the complete data subgroup, uSCIT was found to be significantly more effective than placebo, with improvements in the CSMS of 13.4% (P = 0.0038) and 26.9% (P = 0.0031) for the whole population and complete data groups, respectively. There was a similar pattern for symptom scores alone (eyes and nose), with improvements for uSCIT compared with placebo of 10.9% (P = 0.0132) and 24.7% (P = 0.0181) for the whole population and complete data groups, respectively. Conclusion: The disparity in the primary endpoint between the whole population and the subgroup with complete data was considerable. Although a significant benefit for uSCIT compared with placebo was detected in each set of data, the size of the effect was approximately doubled when complete data were used to compare the treatment groups. It is therefore apparent that using the matched pairs method to compensate for incomplete data may not improve the precision of the estimate of treatment effect for the whole population, in this case yielding a 50% underestimate of treatment efficacy in approximately one third of subjects. This phenomenon represents a significant challenge in the assessment of SIT formulations for allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

An abbreviated dose escalation scheme of a high-dose sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) Single Dose Preparation is safe and convenient in adults and children; Background: A new generation of highdose sublingual immunotherapy was launched in 2006. Data from a doubleblind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial verified the statistically significant and clinically relevant efficacy and good tolerability of the grass-pollen preparation. The study dose escalation (on one day) stipulated three applications of increasing doses with a total waiting period of 150 min (60/60/30). To obtain data on safety of an abbreviated dose escalation scheme used in daily practice in a large number of patients, data were retrospectively collected in an observational study. Methods: A structured 4-sided questionnaire was used to collect data of 345 subjects suffering from IgE-mediated allergy to grass pollen from 83 office-based specialist's practices. The documentation comprised amongst others patients' case history, dose escalation scheme and adverse reactions (AR). Moreover, physicians assessed tolerability of initial therapy by means of a visual analogue scale (VAS), ranging from 1 (very good) to 10 (very bad) and convenience in daily practice via choice boxes (unproblematical to integration not possible). Results: 50% male and 50% female patients aged 5 to 75 years (mean 30.4 years) were included. 9% of them were children (5 to 11 years) and another 9% were young adults (12-17 years). 333 (97%) of subjects received the individual maintenance dose on the first day. In 50% of the cases the escalation scheme was abbreviated by the doctors from suggested 60 min waiting period between the doses to just 15 min. The overall safety was very good: only mild to moderate AR were observed during dose escalation - most frequently oral allergy syndrome (e.g. allergic symptoms, lip swelling or itching, prickle under the tongue), no serious adverse reactions. Children and young adults showed the same frequency of ARs as adults. The overall tolerability was stated by the physicians (via VAS) with 1.98 in the average. The Chi square-test of the different escalation schemes showed no significant difference in appearance of ARs. Conclusion: The high-dose SLIT Single Dose preparation (AllerSlit forte) is convenient and safe to administer within the doctor's practice during the short escalation phase.

Results: Symptom and medication scores were further improved during the third treatment year in comparison to the year before. Relation between grass pollen exposure and efficacy for a grass allergen immunotherapy tablet; Background: Pollen levels display extreme day-to-day variation. Hence, post hoc analyses exploring the effect of grass pollen exposure on efficacy measures and observed differences between treatment groups were performed for a phase III trial investigating the efficacy and safety in children of the once-daily ALK grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense, 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU). Methods: A total of 253 children aged 5-16 years with grass allergy were randomised 1 : 1 to receive either active treatment or placebo prior to and throughout the grass pollen season 2007. Symptomatic medications were provided as rescue medication to both groups in a step-wise fashion. Statistical analyses of efficacy parameters were performed with two different definitions of the pollen season, using 10 or 30 grains/m3 as threshold. In addition, the effect of pollen exposure was explored by investigating the efficacy for days with low, medium and high pollen counts and by modelling the dependence of the efficacy scores on the pollen count for each treatment group. Results: Statistically significant differences between active and placebo demonstrated effect of the ALK grass AIT throughout the entire grass pollen season for both pollen season definitions. The definition of the pollen season influenced the efficacy outcome. Using 10 grains/m3, the relative differences between active and placebo were 22% for both the mean symptom score and for well days. These differences increased upon replacing the threshold with 30 grains/m3, to 28% for the symptom score and 44% for well days. On days with high pollen counts (>50 grains/m3), symptoms increased compared to days with low pollen counts (≤10 grains/m3), from a daily average of 2.1 to 3.8 for the placebo group and from 1.7 to 2.7 for the active group. Simultaneously the average medication score increased from 0.8 to 2.4 for the placebo group but only from 0.4 to 0.9 for the active group. Modelling of the efficacy scores showed a substantial increase in the difference between active and placebo upon increasing pollen load. Conclusion: This was the first phase III trial investigating the ALK grass AIT in children. A clear statistically significant difference between active and placebo was seen throughout the entire grass pollen season, in favour of active treatment. On days with high pollen counts the clinical benefit of the ALK grass AIT was markedly increased, both for symptoms and for the use of symptomatic medication.
Treatment with a grass allergen immunotherapy tablet in children above and below the age of 10 - efficacy, safety and immunological response; Background: Treatment with the ALK grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (Phleum pratense, 75,000 SQ-T/2,800 BAU), is efficacious and well-tolerated in adult grass-allergic patients. Methods: A total of 253 children aged 5-16 years with grass allergy were randomised 1 : 1 to receive either active treatment or placebo prior to and throughout the grass pollen season 2007. Symptomatic medications were provided as rescue medication to both groups. The population was divided into two age groups comprising 140 children aged 5-10 years and 113 children aged 11-16 years. The effect of age on efficacy was also analysed by including age as a covariate in the symptom score analysis. Results: Including age as a covariate in the symptom score analysis indicated age to have no influence on the efficacy, as demonstrated by a P-value of 0.6 for the interaction between age and treatment. Analysis of the difference between active and placebo for each age group showed a slightly higher relative difference in symptom score for the younger children compared with the older, 26% versus 19%. The difference between active and placebo was statistically significant for the 5-10 year old (P = 0.047) although the trial was powered for analysis of the population as a whole. In the active group the percentage of adverse events (AEs) assessed as treatment-related was nominally lower for the younger group than for the older children, 32% versus 40%. The percentages of AEs assessed as moderate or severe in the active group were similar for the two age groups. For both active and placebo, the overall number of AEs was nominally higher in the younger group than in the older group. The immunological response (IgE, IgG4 and IgE-blocking factor) was similar for the two age groups. There was a tendency for the younger group towards an increased response in IgE-blocking factor with onset of the grass pollen season, evident in both the actively treated and the placebo group. Conclusion: This was the first phase III trial investigating the ALK grass AIT in children. Once-daily administration was found to be clinically efficacious and welltolerated. The effect was comparable for children below and above the age of 10, as was the safety pattern and the immunological response.

Recombinant timothy grass pollen allergen Phl p 5.0109: Physicochemical characterisation of the proposed international standardisation reference molecule; Background: Group five allergens are major allergens of grasses. Together with group 1 allergens they account for the majority of IgE-reactivity in sera of grass allergic subjects. The Phl p 5 allergens are a heterogeneous group of proteins comprising of two isoallergens (Phl p 5a and Phl p 5b) with several variants. Phl p 5.0109 is a representative for Phl p 5a, and a recombinant preparation has been chosen as a reference molecule in the international standardization project, CREATE. Recombinant Phl p 5.0109 has also been used in clinical trials of allergen specific immunotherapy as part of a recombinant allergen cocktail. Methods: Purified recombinant Phl p 5.0109 has been analysed by SDS-PAGE, Western Blot, IEF, SEC-MALS, AF4- MALS, N-terminal sequencing, MALDI- MS and MS/MS peptide mapping. Amino acid analysis, refractive index (RI) measurements and the Edelhoch method have been used to measure the molar absorption coefficient ε necessary for spectrophotometric protein concentration determinations. Results: Purified Phl p 5.0109 appears as a homogeneous preparation as shown by single bands in SDS-PAGE, Western blot and IEF. Mass determination by light scattering experiments (MALS) proves the monomeric state of rPhl p 5.0109. The ε- determinations yielded comparable results with Edelhoch and RI-based methods, which differ from those of sequence based prediction methods and from amino acid analysis. Conclusion: Recombinant Phl p 5.0109 is a well-characterised candidate suitable as a reference standard for allergen quantification as well as for allergen specific immunotherapy using recombinant allergens.
Epitope-specific immunisation with a mimotope gene vaccine of Phl p 5; Background: A DNA vaccine encoding the mimotope of grass pollen major allergen Phl p 5 was constructed. Methods: To prove whether the mimotope gene can induce an allergen-specific immune response, naive BALB/c mice were immunized s.c. either with the construct alone or linked to a Tetanus toxin T-helper epitope. Moreover, two immunization strategies were compared, i.e. gene gun bombardment versus intradermal injection. Results: Intradermal and gene gun application of both mimotope constructs elicited Phl p 5-specific antibody responses. Gene gun bombardment induced a Th2 biased immune response, typically associated with IgG1 and IgE antibody production. In contrast, intradermal injection induced blocking antibodies which were able to inhibit allergen-specific cross-linking of IgE in an RBL assay. Whereas the DNA construct encoding the full length Phl p 5 was shown to activate allergen-specific T cells and thereby IL-4 and IFN-γ production, the mimotope constructs being devoid of allergen-specific T-cell epitopes were not able to stimulate cytokine production. Conclusion: Intradermal injection of a mimotope gene induced a Th1 biased immune response accompanied by the induction of blocking IgG antibodies and devoid of allergen-specific T cell activation. We therefore suggest that mimotope gene vaccines are suitable candidates for epitope-specific immunotherapy.

Serum-specific IgE/total IgE ratio and clinical response to allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: To date, no predictive tests for the clinical response to allergen-specific immunotherapy (ASI) are available. Therefore, an in vivo or in vitro test would be of great value. Objective: To evaluate pre-treatment parameters used in diagnosing allergic rhinitis, serum specific IgE (s-IgE), serum total IgE (t-IgE) as well as blood eosinophil counts (b-eos), to identify if any predict clinical improvement in mono-sensitized patients with allergic rhinitis with or without asthma treated with immunotherapy. Phleum pratense alone is sufficient for allergen-specific immunotherapy against allergy to Pooideae grass pollens; Background Specific immunotherapy is the only causal treatment of allergy available today. Traditionally, therapeutic products based on either a single grass species or a mix of such extracts are used for grass pollen immunotherapy. Investigations comparing the immunological response to these allergen preparations are needed to ensure optimal treatment. The objective of this study was to investigate patterns of T and B cell cross-reactivity to Pooideae single-species extracts and to extract mixes. Methods IgG4 induced by immunotherapy with Phleum pratense extract was investigated for cross-reactivity using nine single-species extracts and four mixes. For the mixes, studies of IgE cross-reactivity were also performed. T cell cross-reactivity was investigated in lines specific to nPhl p 1 or nPhl p 5 allergens, and the amounts of group 1 and 5 allergens in the extracts were quantified by a single radial immunodiffusion. Results The levels of treatment-induced IgG4 detected by all the extracts displayed a clear correlation to that detected by the P. pratense pollen extract. The IgE studies confirmed the cross-reactivity of P. pratense-specific B cells towards the allergens contained in the mixes, and the T cell studies demonstrated cross-reactivity towards group 1 and 5 major allergens in extracts of six temperate grass species. Conclusion Extensive T and B cell cross-reactivity was observed towards the allergens of the Pooideae grasses, and the degree of B cell cross-reactivity was independent of the number of species included in the extract mixes. This implies that treatment with pollen extract of just one Pooideae species will affect the allergic responses caused by any of the temperate grasses in this subfamily. © 2009 Blackwell Publishing Ltd.
Mechanisms of sublingual immunotherapy; Allergen-specific sublingual immunotherapy is now recognized to be an efficacious and well-tolerated treatment for allergic rhinitis. Emerging treatment strategies are also aimed at the primary treatment of allergic asthma, particularly allergy to house dust mites. Knowledge of the exact mechanisms of action of sublingual immunotherapy is at a basic level, although there appear to be similarities to the immunological changes seen in subcutaneous immunotherapy. An improved understanding should allow the development of more effective treatment programs and widen the potential use of this form of immunotherapy. This review discusses the possible mechanism of action of sublingual immunotherapy, including data from animal and clinical studies, while comparing this with the current understanding of subcutaneous immunotherapy.
Evaluation of serum s-IgE/total IgE ratio in predicting clinical response to allergen-specific immunotherapy; Background: To date, no predictive tests for the clinical response to allergen-specific immunotherapy (ASI) are available. Therefore an in vivo or in vitro test would be of great value. Objective: We sought to evaluate pretreatment parameters used in diagnosing allergic rhinitis and determining serum specific IgE (s-IgE) levels, serum total IgE (t-IgE) levels, and blood eosinophil counts and to identify whether can be used to predict clinical improvement in monosensitized patients with allergic rhinitis with or without asthma treated with immunotherapy. Methods: We analyzed 279 patients who had undergone 4 years of ASI administered either by means of the subcutaneous immunotherapy (76 patients) or sublingual immunotherapy (203 patients) routes. Serum t-IgE and s-IgE levels, blood eosinophil counts, and serum s-IgE/t-IgE ratios were calculated and tested for correlation with clinical response to ASI. Receiver operating characteristic curves were determined. Predicted probabilities and predictive areas under the curve were calculated. Results: The clinical response to ASI was effective in 145 (52.0%) of 279 total patients, 42 (55.2%) of 76 patients treated with subcutaneous immunotherapy, and 103 (50.7%) of 203 patients treated with sublingual immunotherapy. A significant correlation was found between the serum s-IgE/t-IgE ratio and the clinical response to ASI, with high ratios (>16.2) associated with an effective response. The sensitivity and specificity of the area under the curve of the ratio were higher than those of serum s-IgE and t-IgE alone. Conclusion: The calculation of the serum s-IgE/t-IgE ratio for predicting the clinical response to ASI offers an advantage over measuring t-IgE and s-IgE levels in monosensitized patients for the following allergens: grass, Parietaria judaica, Olea europea, and house dust mite. © 2009 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology.
An economic evaluation of grazax for the treatment of grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis in children; OBJECTIVES: To determine the cost-effectiveness of the grass allergen immunotherapy tablet (AIT), Grazax (ALK-Abelló A/S) for the treatment of grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis in children either with or without co-existing asthma. The analysis compares treatment using Grazax in combination with symptomatic medications, to using symptomatic medications alone in terms of costs and health outcomes. METHODS: The model uses a decision tree structure to evaluate two grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis treatments for a cohort of 1000 hypothetical children. The analysis is performed from the perspective of the payer, including only direct costs in the base case. Treatment is modelled in terms of the management of symptoms, reduction in resource use and averting the development of allergic asthma. The evaluation is UK-based and models both short- and long-term effects. Several data inputs, such as resource use and probabilities, are drawn from the paediatric GT-12 clinical trial and the Preventive Allergy Treatment (PAT) study. Cost data are sourced from established published sources and utility values are derived using GT-12 trial data and a published study. RESULTS: Treatment with Grazax in combination with symptomatic medications compared to treatment with symptomatic medications alone generates a (discounted) incremental cost per QALY gained of 10,007GBP ($14,578, ε11,034), for the base case time horizon of nine years. The QALY gains are a result of increased quality of life related to effective symptom management. The sensitivity analysis carried out around key parameters (e.g. unit costs, medication costs, probabilities, utilities) shows that the results estimated by the model remain robust. CONCLUSIONS: Grazax has been shown to improve patient outcomes, at an increased cost. The resulting incremental cost per QALY falls below commonly accepted willingness to pay thresholds. Therefore, Grazax is a cost-effective option for the treatment of grass pollen induced rhinoconjunctivitis in the UK paediatric population.
Reducing allergenicity by altering allergen fold: A mosaic protein of Phl p 1 for allergy vaccination; Background: The major timothy grass pollen allergen, Phl p 1, resembles the allergenic epitopes of natural group I grass pollen allergens and is recognized by more than 95% of grass-pollen-allergic patients. Our objective was the construction, purification and immunologic characterization of a genetically modified derivative of the major timothy grass pollen allergen, Phl p 1 for immunotherapy of grass pollen allergy. Methods: A mosaic protein was generated by PCR-based re-assembly and expression of four cDNAs coding for Phl p 1 fragments and compared to the Phl p 1 wild-type by circular dichroism analysis, immunoglobulin E (IgE)-binding capacity, basophil activation assays and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay competition assays. Immune responses to the derivative were studied in BALB/c mice. Results: Grass-pollen-allergic patients exhibited greater than an 85% reduction in IgE reactivity to the mosaic as compared with the Phl p 1 allergen and basophil activation experiments confirmed the reduced allergenic activity of the mosaic. It also induced less Phl p 1-specific IgE antibodies than Phl p 1 upon immunization of mice. However, immunization of mice and rabbits with the mosaic induced IgG antibodies that inhibited patients' IgE-binding to the wild-type allergen and Phl p 1-induced degranulation of basophils. Conclusion: We have developed a strategy based on rational molecular reassembly to convert one of the clinically most relevant allergens into a hypoallergenic derivative for allergy vaccination. © 2009 Blackwell Munksgaard.

Implementation of pre-seasonal sublingual immunotherapy with a five-grass pollen tablet during optimal dosage assessment; Background: The optimal dose (300IR) of a five-grass pollen sublingual immunotherapy tablet in terms of efficacy was previously demonstrated from the first pollen season. Objective: Here, we aim to confirm whether this dose remained optimal during the peak of the pollen season by assessing the efficacy and quality of life data. Methods: A total of 628 subjects with grass pollen rhinoconjunctivitis were randomized in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, pan-European trial. Subjects received once-daily tablets (Stallergenes, Antony, France) of 100IR, 300IR, 500IR or placebo, starting 4 months before and throughout the 2005 grass pollen season. The pollen season was defined as the first day of 3 consecutive days with a grass pollen count above 30 grains/m3 of air, recorded using Hirst-type volumetric pollen traps, to the last day before 3 consecutive days with a pollen count below 30 grains/m3. Results: The grass pollen season lasted an average of 30 days, with a peak of 12 days. The mean treatment duration before the grass pollen season was similar in the four treatment groups (121.4±31.1 to 128.6±15.4 days in the safety population). Both the 300IR and 500IR groups had highly significant improvements in Rhinoconjunctivitis Total Symptom Score (RTSS) vs. placebo at the peak pollen season (P=0.0005 and 0.0014, respectively), which agreed with improvements in RTSS in the primary evaluations. The average RTSS scores were slightly elevated during the peak pollen season in all treatment groups. The overall Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire score confirmed the optimal dosage 300IR at peak (P<0.0001) and at the end (P≤0.0031) of the pollen season. All doses were well tolerated. Conclusion: At the peak pollen season, the efficacy and quality of life data for both 300IR and 500IR groups was significantly improved vs. the placebo group. These results confirm the conclusions of the primary evaluations and validate the use of 300IR tablets for clinical practice. © 2008 Stallergenes.

Clinical utility of sublingual immunotherapy in pediatric patients with allergic rhinitis and/or asthma; Although sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) is a common adjuvant treatment for allergic rhinitis and allergic asthma in Europe, it is used minimally in the United States because of lack of approval by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of allergen extracts for sublingual treatment and inconsistent study findings on extract potency, dosing levels, and dosing schedules. Data are particularly lacking on use of SLIT in pediatric patients, who may represent a potential patient population for this type of immunotherapy delivery because of its favorable safety and acceptability to children compared to subcutaneous immunotherapy (SCIT). Differences in the mechanism of action of SLIT compared to SCIT may also confer some treatment and safety advantages. Clinical trials on SLIT in pediatric patients have provided inconsistent results, but this inconsistency may be due in part to less than optimum dosing and durations of treatment. The appeal of SLIT as a treatment in children is further enhanced by its potential for possibly preventing progression to asthma if initiated at a young age. This article reviews the clinical evidence on studies in pediatric populations regarding efficacy and safety, and its implications in the treatment of allergic rhinitis and allergic asthma in children. © 2009 Mary Ann Liebert, Inc.

Evaluation of a compliance device in a subgroup of adult patients receiving specific immunotherapy with grass allergen tablets (GRAZAX®) in a randomized, open-label, controlled study: An a priori subgroup analysis; Objectives: This a priori subgroup analysis was conducted to assess patients' experience with a compliance device for the administration of sublingual specific immunotherapy for grass pollen-induced rhinoconjunctivitis. Methods: The present paper reports the results of a subgroup analysis of a multicenter, randomized, controlled, open-label European study in which adults with grass pollen-induced rhinoconjunctivitis received once-daily treatment with grass allergen tablets with or without a device to aid compliance. Treatment was given ~6 to 12 weeks before the grass pollen season, during the season (~8-10 weeks), and for up to 2 weeks after the end of the season. In the subgroup analysis, patients from Germany and the Netherlands who had been randomized to receive the compliance device were asked to complete a brief questionnaire at the final study visit. The questionnaire included 6 items concerning patients' use of the device and whether it helped them remember to take their tablets. Results: Of the 91 patients from Germany and the Netherlands who were randomized to use the compliance device along with grass allergen tablets, 71 returned the questionnaire. Among responders, 58 of 71 (82%) reported using the device sometimes or always, 50 of 63 (79%) found the device easy to use, 32 of 69 (46%) found that the device made it easier to remember to take tablets, and 43 of 71 (61%) indicated that they would consider using the device again. Conclusion: Most patients in this subgroup analysis used the compliance device as a medication reminder and rated it easy to use. © 2009 Excerpta Medica Inc. All rights reserved.
